About this book. I wrote this as a free, evidence-based companion to the System of Inevitability, which I created. The material on altered-state practice comes from my own account and philosophy, and from a project document, compiled in November 2026, that discusses geometric expression in the martial arts without naming any particular system. This book does not recommend that anyone use any substance. Curiosity about practice while altered is not a recommendation to take a substance, and it is not a syllabus. Where this book suggests practices, safeguards, or tests, those are my suggestions, informed by the general scientific literature. The plates and diagrams are original drawings made for this book.

Health, legal, and harm-reduction notice. This book is for education, reflection, and harm reduction. It is not medical, psychological, or legal advice, and it does not encourage anyone to use any drug. Psilocybin is a controlled substance in most countries, and possessing or using it is a crime in most places. A small number of jurisdictions have created regulated or decriminalized frameworks; the details differ and change, and you must learn the law where you are. This book contains no information on doses, sources, or preparation. Psilocybin can cause intense anxiety, confusion, and impaired coordination and timing, and it carries specific medical and psychiatric risks (Chapter 5). If you choose to explore altered states, you are responsible for the choice, and for the safety of everyone around you.

About the science. Every study cited here was checked against its published record (authors, year, journal, and DOI) at the time of writing, and the findings reported were checked against the published abstracts. No study, number, or quotation has been invented. Where the evidence is thin or absent, and on the central topic of this book it often is, the text says so.

Dedication

For the curious, who look closely at what is already there.

And for the careful, who make it safe to look.

How to Read This Book

This is the fourth companion to the System of Inevitability. Walking and Turning looked at the system’s conditioning tools. Wave and Return looked at the striking hand. Shape and Choice looked at the mind behind both. This book turns to a different question, one I brought from my own practice: what happens to geometry, touch, timing, and the sense of self when a practitioner trains while perception is altered by psilocybin, and how can that be explored with curiosity and with care?

That question sits at the edge of science. There is a growing body of rigorous research on what psilocybin does to perception, the body, and the sense of self. There is a substantial body of research on the internal martial arts, on touch and pattern, and on contemplative practice. There is almost no research on the place where they meet. So this book has to be especially careful to tell you which kind of knowledge you are reading. You will see three kinds of marked boxes:

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Supported by multiple independent studies, systematic reviews, or meta-analyses with reasonably consistent results. You can lean on these.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive or emerging. Supported by real peer-reviewed research, but the studies are few, small, indirect, or debated. Promising, but hold them loosely.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner experience and philosophy. Experiences, ideas, and suggestions, including my own, that have not been measured. They may be meaningful. They have not been tested. Every practice suggested in Part II falls here.

And the box you should never skip:

⚠ Caution

Caution. Practical safety information, for your body, your mind, and the people around you. Read these.

Citations appear as author and year, for example (Wittmann et al., 2007). The full list, with journal details and DOIs, is in the References. A sentence that makes a factual claim with no citation and no box is my reasonable summary or opinion.

Three kinds of knowledge. Throughout this book, keep three categories apart:

  • Measured: what clinical trials and laboratory studies have found about psilocybin, perception, movement, and practice.
  • Anecdotal: what practitioners, including me, report from their own experience. Real, valuable, and unverified.
  • Speculative: any claim that psilocybin improves martial skill. There is no direct evidence for this, in either direction. Not a single controlled study has tested it.

A word about “responsibly.” My philosophy is to “practice everything altered responsibly.” This book takes both halves of that seriously. Practice everything means curiosity: slow forms, circle walking, free movement, shadow work, light juggling, touch, tracing, and experiments with the senses. Responsibly means the conditions that make that curiosity safe: screening for medical and psychiatric risks, a sober sitter and a safe space, and one firm line about equipment. Heavy implements, the steel-armed dummy at force, live weapons, and sparring with partners are left for sober training, and lighter, softer substitutes take their place. Chapter 5 explains why, from the research on what psilocybin does to coordination and timing.

A word about the “upgrade in human consciousness.” I hope these books will help facilitate an upgrade in human consciousness. Psilocybin research is, in part, a scientific study of exactly that hope: of experiences people describe as among the most meaningful of their lives. Chapter 14 sets out what that research has found, and how much of it is still uncertain.

Foreword

“The purpose is to bring curiosity to practice while altered. Practice everything altered responsibly. This is how you truly understand your mind and body.” — Cory Snell

The first three books in this series were about what the System of Inevitability says. This one begins with something I said.

When I came to write a fourth book, I wrote: “Understandably this crosses into emerging research, but I have used psilocybin while training (unarmed/weapons), juggling, free form, bagwork, and dummy training. It is mindbending.”

That is the whole testimony, and it is mine. I am putting it at the front of the book for two reasons. First, it is honest about where this book comes from: not from a laboratory, but from a practitioner’s own training floor. Second, it is the kind of statement that needs the rest of the book around it. “Mindbending” is a real description of a real experience. It is not yet knowledge.

The source document for this book makes a careful argument. Internal martial arts such as Tai Chi and Baguazhang work with spirals, circles, triangles, and lines that correspond to sound physical principles. Altered perception may make those geometries easier to see and feel: the spiral in the forearm, the circle under the feet, the small deflection that grows into a whole-body turn. And the attitude it recommends is “recognition rather than invention”: the geometry is already latent in good movement, waiting to be noticed.

My own view goes a step further. I think the altered state is not only a source of insights to take home. It is a place to study: to watch your own balance, timing, attention, fear, and sense of self change, and to learn from the changes. That is what most of this book is about.

It is also why I have tried to be rigorous about the research. The same studies that describe the richness of psilocybin perception also describe slower timing, poorer balance, and impaired psychomotor performance. Those findings are why this book draws its one firm line: it does not recommend weapons, heavy implements, or forceful dummy work in an altered state, even though my own training has included them. They are not a reason to stop being curious. They are a reason to choose the right tools for a curious session: soft balls, light sticks, foam blades, an open floor, a sober friend.

Read it slowly. Keep the categories apart: what is measured, what is felt, and what is merely hoped. And share what you find.

Cory Snell November 2026

Part I · The Lens

The geometry is already in the movement. The question is how to see it, and how to know when what you see is real.

An Invitation to Curiosity

Chapter 1

The core training stance is recognition rather than invention. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Every serious practitioner eventually wants to know what is really happening inside their own movement. Where does the turn begin? What does the back foot do when the hand redirects a push? What happens to balance when attention drifts, or to timing when fear rises? Most of the time we cannot see these things clearly. They are too fast, too familiar, or too deeply automatic.

This book is about one unusual way of looking: practising while perception is altered by psilocybin, the active compound in so-called magic mushrooms, and treating the experience as a chance to study one’s own mind and body. It is also about the ordinary, sober ways of looking that have far more research behind them. And it is about how to tell the difference between a pattern you have genuinely discovered and a pattern your brain has made up.

Where this book comes from

The series these books belong to grew out of the System of Inevitability, which I created. This fourth book draws on two different sources, and it is important to keep them separate.

The first is a project document that discusses geometric expression in the martial arts without naming any specific system. It describes the circles and spirals of the internal Chinese arts; the physics of angular momentum and rotational inertia; how shifts in perception (visual pattern recognition, proprioception, and interoception) “can make these geometric qualities more available during practice”; how such insights might be carried into regular training; and a set of safety boundaries. Its central stance is “recognition rather than invention: the geometries are treated as already latent in efficient movement and are refined through repeated, attentive practice.”

The second is my own testimony and philosophy, set out in the Foreword: years of training that have included practice under psilocybin, and a conviction that practising altered, responsibly, “is how you truly understand your mind and body.”

This book does not recommend that anyone use any substance. Curiosity about practice while altered is not a recommendation to take a substance, and it is not a syllabus.

The honest state of the evidence

Here is the single most important sentence in this book: there are essentially no scientific studies of martial arts practice, or of skilled movement training of any kind, under psilocybin.

A 2025 review asking whether psychedelics have a place in sport concluded that their effects on athletic performance “remain largely unknown,” and that studies of their effects on muscle strength, motor coordination, endurance, and related factors “are still scarce” (Portes et al., 2025). Surveys show that some athletes use psychedelics and that many are open to supervised psychedelic therapy (VanderZwaag et al., 2024; Portes & Bertoglio, 2026), but surveys of attitudes tell us nothing about what happens to a Tai Chi form or a bag drill.

What does exist is a substantial body of laboratory research on what psilocybin does to perception, time, the body, the sense of self, and psychomotor performance. There is good research on Tai Chi and, to a lesser extent, on other internal arts. There is a deep literature on pattern recognition, touch, and the learning of skill. And there is a growing body of work on meditation and other contemplative practices that touch some of the same experiences. This book brings those bodies of knowledge together, and is clear about the gaps between them.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Psychedelics and sport: almost no data. The effects of psychedelics on athletic performance remain largely unknown, and studies of their effects on strength, coordination, and endurance are scarce (Portes et al., 2025). No controlled study has examined martial arts training under psilocybin.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

My philosophy. “The purpose is to bring curiosity to practice while altered. Practice everything altered responsibly. This is how you truly understand your mind and body.” This is a practitioner’s view, offered with conviction. It has not been tested, and this book presents it as philosophy, alongside the evidence that bears on it.

What this book will and will not do

This book will describe, as fully as the evidence allows, what psilocybin is known to do to perception, timing, balance, touch, and self-experience. It will describe what to notice and explore during an altered practice session, if you choose to have one: slow forms, circle walking, free movement, shadow work, light juggling with soft balls, light touch on the bag and dummy, tracing spirals, and experiments with the senses. It will set out what “responsibly” means: screening, a sitter, a safe space, and lighter tools. And it will show how to check whether what you found is real.

This book will not give doses, sources, or preparation methods. It will not give legal advice. It will not claim that psilocybin makes anyone a better martial artist, because nobody knows. And it will not pretend that the altered state is the only door. Chapter 13 describes sober practices that reach many of the same qualities: geometric awareness, a quieter self, and deeper attention to the body.

How the book is arranged

Part I, The Lens, describes the geometry of the internal arts and the evidence behind them (Chapter 2), what psilocybin does to perception and the sense of self (Chapter 3), and what it does to the moving body (Chapter 4).

Part II, Practising Altered, begins with what “responsibly” means (Chapter 5), then describes what to explore in slow forms and circle walking (Chapter 6), in free movement, shadow work, and light juggling (Chapter 7), in touch with the bag and the dummy (Chapter 8), and in the inner senses (Chapter 9).

Part III, Pattern, explains how brains find patterns and how experts see them (Chapter 10), and how to check whether a pattern is real (Chapter 11).

Part IV, Carrying It Home, covers integration (Chapter 12), sober paths to the same qualities (Chapter 13), and what research says about psilocybin, meaning, and consciousness (Chapter 14).

If you read only three chapters, read 4, 5, and 11.

⚠ Caution

This book is not an invitation to use drugs. If you have never used psilocybin, nothing here suggests you should. If you have a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder, take lithium, or have heart disease, read Chapter 5 before anything else. And if you do practise altered, never do it alone.

Geometry in the Internal Arts

Chapter 2

Circular and spiral trajectories in Tai Chi for yielding, redirecting force, and generating power with minimal effort through elliptical and spiraling pathways. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

The source document begins with the geometry of the internal Chinese martial arts. Tai Chi works with “circular and spiral trajectories” for “yielding, redirecting force, and generating power with minimal effort.” Baguazhang is built on “circle walking and continuous spiraling palm changes,” with “constant transformation and connection to a central axis.” Many arts use “triangular structures for stability, straight lines for direct power, and curved redirections for efficiency.” And these geometries, the document says, “correspond to principles of angular momentum, rotational inertia, conservation of energy, and paths of least resistance.”

Before asking how altered perception might change the experience of these shapes, it is worth knowing what is actually known about the arts themselves.

The physics, briefly

The physical principles the document names are real, and they are worth stating plainly.

Angular momentum is the rotational equivalent of momentum: the product of how fast something spins and how its mass is distributed around the axis. Without an outside twisting force, it stays constant. That is why a skater spins faster when the arms come in.

Rotational inertia (the moment of inertia) is how hard it is to change something’s rotation. Mass far from the axis increases it; mass close to the axis reduces it. A whole body turning with the arms close is easier to start and stop than one turning with the arms extended.

Triangles are stable because a triangle cannot change its shape without changing the length of a side. A stance with a wide, triangulated base resists being pushed over more than a narrow one.

Curves redirect. A force that meets a curved surface at an angle can be deflected rather than absorbed head-on, as anyone who has pushed against a turning door knows.

None of this is mystical, and none of it guarantees that a particular form uses these principles well. But it does mean that the language of spirals and circles in the internal arts is describing something physically meaningful.

What Tai Chi has been shown to do

Tai Chi is one of the most studied movement practices in the world, especially for older adults.

Balance and falls. In an early randomized trial in people aged 70 and over, Tai Chi reduced the risk of multiple falls by 47.5% after adjusting for fall risk factors (Wolf et al., 1996). A 2017 meta-analysis of 18 trials with 3,824 participants found that Tai Chi was associated with a lower chance of falling at least once (risk ratio 0.80) and a lower rate of falls (rate ratio 0.69), with a possible effect of publication bias (Huang et al., 2017). The Cochrane review of exercise for falls prevention rated the evidence that Tai Chi reduces the number of people who fall as high-certainty, and its effect on the rate of falls as low-certainty (Sherrington et al., 2019). In a trial of 670 adults aged 70 or over at high risk of falling, a therapeutic Tai Ji Quan programme reduced falls substantially compared with stretching, and by 31% compared with a multimodal exercise programme (Li et al., 2018). In people with mild-to-moderate Parkinson’s disease, Tai Chi improved measures of postural stability more than resistance training or stretching (Li et al., 2012).

Proprioception. Long-term older Tai Chi practitioners made smaller errors than matched controls when repositioning the knee, and could lean further without losing stability (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003). In another comparison, older Tai Chi practitioners detected smaller passive movements at the ankle than both sedentary people and long-term swimmers or runners (Xu et al., 2004).

Cognition and wellbeing. A meta-analysis of 20 studies found that Tai Chi shows potential to enhance cognitive function in older adults, especially executive function, though trial quality was modest (Wayne et al., 2014). In randomized trials in people with fibromyalgia, Tai Chi improved symptoms more than wellness education and stretching (Wang et al., 2010) and as much as or more than aerobic exercise (Wang et al., 2018).

● Evidence: well-established

Tai Chi improves balance and reduces falls in older adults. Randomized trials and meta-analyses support this (Wolf et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Sherrington et al., 2019). Long-term practitioners show better joint position sense and movement detection (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003; Xu et al., 2004).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Benefits for cognition and chronic pain are promising. Tai Chi may enhance executive function in older adults (Wayne et al., 2014) and improved fibromyalgia symptoms in randomized trials (Wang et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2018).

A complex practice

Why does Tai Chi work? Researchers have pointed out that this is a hard question. Tai Chi integrates many physical, cognitive, and ritual components at once: slow weight shifting, attention to the body, breathing, imagery, a teacher, a group, a philosophy. That richness makes it difficult to design a fair placebo and to attribute outcomes to any single ingredient (Wayne & Kaptchuk, 2008). An earlier review found Tai Chi studies on balance scattered and inconsistent, with wide variation in measures, populations, and styles (Wu, 2002). The evidence has grown much stronger since, but the question of which part does the work is still open.

That matters for this book. If someone feels that a spiral became clearer in an altered state, the experience is entangled with attention, slowness, expectation, mood, and setting, just as Tai Chi’s benefits are entangled with all its components.

Push hands and the felt line of force

Tai Chi’s two-person practice, push hands, is the closest the internal arts come to a laboratory of “listening, blending, and following natural lines of force,” as the source document puts it. Remarkably little research exists on it. In a biomechanical case study, an experienced master defended pushes from four opponents while his movement, muscle activity, and ground forces were recorded. He used a subtle postural adjustment: weight shifted from front to rear foot, the centre of gravity shifted sideways, the upper-body muscles stayed quiet, and the rear leg took the incoming force. Inexperienced people doing the same task all lost their balance (Chen et al., 2010). It is a single case, but it shows what yielding and redirecting force can look like when measured.

Circle walking and Wing Chun

Baguazhang has barely been studied. In a 2026 randomized trial, 46 sedentary postmenopausal women were assigned to twelve weeks of supervised Baguazhang or to their usual lifestyle. Circle walking was the most demanding part of each session, at moderate cardiovascular intensity, and systolic blood pressure was lower after the programme than in the control group. The authors note that the study shows Baguazhang is a feasible, moderate-intensity exercise, not that it is superior to other exercise (Cao & Zhang, 2026).

Wing Chun, the art most associated with the wooden dummy, has a similarly thin research base. An early study found that continuous Wing Chun practice demanded more oxygen and raised the heart rate more than Tai Chi, enough to provide a cardiorespiratory training effect for people starting with low fitness (Schneider & Leung, 1991). A motion-capture study of four experienced practitioners compared two ways of sequencing straight punches in a modern Wing Chun style and found that both showed proximal-to-distal sequencing of peak joint speeds, with different timing and fist speeds (Fuchs et al., 2017). An essay has proposed a psychological framework linking Wing Chun’s principles to wellbeing, but it is a conceptual proposal, not an experiment (Watson & Kemp, 2025). Chapter 8 returns to the dummy itself.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

The other internal arts are barely studied. A single trial suggests Baguazhang is a feasible moderate-intensity exercise (Cao & Zhang, 2026). Wing Chun research consists of a few small physiological and biomechanical studies (Schneider & Leung, 1991; Fuchs et al., 2017). Push hands has been examined in a single biomechanical case study (Chen et al., 2010).

Recognition rather than invention

The source document’s most useful idea is its stance: “recognition rather than invention.” The geometries “are treated as already latent in efficient movement and are refined through repeated, attentive practice.”

This is a scientifically sensible attitude. Book 3 described how the nervous system’s own movements follow curved, smooth, lawful paths, and how skilled movement allows variation where it does not matter. A spiral is not something the practitioner imposes on the body. It is something the body already tends to do when it moves well. The task is to notice it, and then to refine it.

It is also, as later chapters will show, a protective attitude. A practitioner who expects to recognize what is already in good movement will check every new insight against the movement itself, on film and in sober practice. A practitioner who expects to invent a new geometry in an altered state is far more likely to be fooled.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“These geometries correspond to principles of angular momentum, rotational inertia, conservation of energy, and paths of least resistance.” The physics is real. Whether a particular form or practitioner uses it efficiently has to be measured case by case. “Paths of least resistance” is a useful image rather than a measured property of the internal arts.

What Psilocybin Does to Perception and Self

Chapter 3

Visual–kinesthetic bridging: Perceiving movement trajectories as spirals, figure-eights, or continuous loops. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Psilocybin is a compound produced by several species of mushroom. In the body it is converted to psilocin, which acts mainly by stimulating a particular serotonin receptor, the 5-HT2A receptor. Controlled studies have shown that blocking this receptor with a drug called ketanserin prevents many of psilocybin’s effects, including its psychosis-like state (Vollenweider et al., 1998) and its visual hallucinations (Kometer et al., 2013).

This chapter describes what laboratory research has measured about the experience. It is the background for everything in Part II: if you are going to study your own mind and body in this state, you need to know what the state is known to do.

Profound, mostly pleasant, sometimes frightening

The largest pooled analysis of laboratory studies combined raw data from eight double-blind, placebo-controlled experiments in 110 healthy people. Psilocybin produced dose-dependent, “profound changes in mood, perception, thought and self-experience,” yet most participants described the experience as “pleasurable, enriching and non-threatening.” Acute adverse reactions, meaning strong dysphoria or anxiety and panic, occurred only at the two highest doses, in a relatively small proportion of people, and all were managed with interpersonal support. Follow-up found no persisting perception disorders, prolonged psychosis, or long-term impairment in anyone (Studerus et al., 2011).

Those participants were healthy, screened, well prepared, and carefully monitored. That context matters enormously, and Chapter 5 returns to it. In another laboratory study, at the higher doses studied, 39% of volunteers had episodes of extreme anxiety or fear (Griffiths et al., 2011).

Researchers measure these experiences with questionnaires. A standard altered states of consciousness rating scale, evaluated on pooled data from 43 experimental studies, was refined into eleven more specific lower-order scales (Studerus et al., 2010). The Mystical Experience Questionnaire measures mystical-type experiences (Barrett et al., 2015). The Ego-Dissolution Inventory measures the loss of the ordinary sense of self (Nour et al., 2016).

● Evidence: well-established

Psilocybin produces dose-dependent changes in perception, mood, thought, and self-experience, via the 5-HT2A receptor. In screened, prepared, monitored laboratory volunteers, most experiences were described as positive, but anxiety and panic occurred, mainly at high doses (Vollenweider et al., 1998; Studerus et al., 2011; Griffiths et al., 2011; Kometer et al., 2013).

Geometry behind the eyes

Of all the effects of psilocybin, the most relevant to a book about geometry is visual. In a double-blind comparison with another hallucinogen, a high dose of psilocybin produced “more frequent, brighter, distinctive, and complex (including textured and kaleidoscopic) images and visions” (Carbonaro et al., 2018).

Many of those images take regular, repeating forms. The psychologist Heinrich Klüver sorted drug-induced geometric hallucinations into four groups he called form constants: (1) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs, and chequer-boards; (2) cobwebs; (3) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones, and vessels; and (4) spirals. In 2001 a team of mathematicians and neuroscientists showed that all four can be explained by the architecture of the primary visual cortex (V1). When the cortex is excited into spontaneous patterns of activity, simple stripes and waves of activity across V1 map onto the visual field, through the eye-to-cortex map, as exactly these shapes: spirals, tunnels, cobwebs, and lattices (Bressloff et al., 2001).

Electrical recordings show what happens on the way. Psilocybin strongly reduced the alpha rhythm over the back of the head, which normally regulates how excitable the visual cortex is, and reduced a visual brain response (the N170) in step with the appearance of visual alterations. All of these effects were blocked by ketanserin. The authors suggest that the visual cortex shifts into a mode in which “stimulus-driven cortical excitation is overwhelmed by spontaneous neuronal excitation” (Kometer et al., 2013).

This is a striking idea for a practitioner of the spiral arts. It suggests that at least some of the geometry seen in the altered state comes not from the world but from the structure of the viewer’s own visual system. That does not make the spirals on a Tai Chi practitioner’s forearm unreal. But it means that a spiral seen during an altered session may be partly the movement and partly the cortex. Chapter 11 describes how to tell them apart.

● Evidence: well-established

Geometric visual imagery is a core psilocybin effect, and its classic forms reflect the architecture of the visual cortex. Psilocybin produces complex, textured, and kaleidoscopic imagery (Carbonaro et al., 2018) through 5-HT2A-dependent changes in visual cortex activity (Kometer et al., 2013). A mathematical model derives Klüver’s four form constants from the organization of V1 (Bressloff et al., 2001).

The quieting of the hubs

Brain imaging shows how far beyond vision the changes go. In an early fMRI study, psilocybin decreased blood flow and activity, most strongly in “hub” regions such as the thalamus and the anterior and posterior cingulate cortex. The decrease in the medial prefrontal cortex predicted the intensity of the subjective effects, and the coupling between the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex, two central nodes of the brain’s default mode network, fell (Carhart-Harris et al., 2012). Book 3 described this network’s link to mind-wandering and self-referential thinking, and how experienced meditators show reduced activity in some of its main nodes (Brewer et al., 2011).

In a related study, the strength of ego dissolution was associated with reduced communication between the medial temporal lobe and high-level cortical regions, a “disintegration” of the salience network, and reduced communication between the brain’s hemispheres (Lebedev et al., 2015).

Two big hypotheses

Two influential theories try to explain these findings. Both are hypotheses.

The entropic brain hypothesis proposes that the psychedelic state is a “primary state” of consciousness with elevated entropy, a richer, less constrained repertoire of brain activity, and that ordinary waking consciousness suppresses entropy in a way that supports reality-testing and self-awareness (Carhart-Harris et al., 2014).

REBUS (relaxed beliefs under psychedelics) combines the entropic brain idea with predictive processing, the view that the brain constantly predicts its sensory input. It proposes that psychedelics “relax the precision of high-level priors or beliefs,” freeing bottom-up information to flow (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019). In plain terms: the brain’s usual assumptions about what it is seeing and feeling loosen their grip.

A more recent proposal, ALBUS (altered beliefs under psychedelics), argues that the opposite can also happen. Under some conditions, prior expectations may become stronger, which would fit the enhanced meaning-making of psychedelic experiences, the “imposition of prior expectations on perception (e.g. hallucinations and pareidolia),” and the delusional thinking that sometimes occurs, including apophenia (Safron et al., 2025).

For a practitioner, the two ideas point to two possibilities that both deserve respect. One is that the loosening of habitual assumptions may let you feel your own movement as if for the first time. The other is that your brain may project patterns onto movement that are not there. The practice chapters assume both are possible.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Entropic brain, REBUS, and ALBUS are hypotheses. They are serious, influential models that organize the imaging data (Carhart-Harris et al., 2014; Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019; Safron et al., 2025), but they have not been established. The specific idea that psilocybin “loosens” a practitioner’s movement habits has not been tested.

Meaning that feels like discovery

Psychedelics also change what matters. In a study with LSD, a related psychedelic, volunteers attributed personal relevance to stimuli that had previously been meaningless to them, an effect blocked by ketanserin (Preller et al., 2017). A theoretical review argues that this “meaning-enhancing” property may help explain the therapeutic, creative, and mystical effects reported with psychedelics (Hartogsohn, 2018).

This is perhaps the single most important fact in this book for anyone hoping to learn from an altered session. The feeling of significance, the sense that this is how the turn really works, is itself one of the things the drug amplifies. It is not proof that the insight is correct. It is also not proof that it is wrong.

The self that steps aside

The source document describes an “ego-dissolution effect on practice”: “Reduced self-referential concern about ‘correct form’ allowing freer exploration of natural trajectories.”

The research supports something close to this, with a qualification. Ego dissolution is a measurable effect (Nour et al., 2016), with identifiable brain correlates (Lebedev et al., 2015). But a careful philosophical and scientific review argues that self-consciousness has many dimensions, including narrative self-talk, memories, and “embodied aspects rooted in multisensory processes,” and that “self-loss” can take several forms. The same review calls for caution about the “problematic conflation of temporary states of self-loss with ‘selflessness’ as a behavioral or social trait” (Millière et al., 2018).

For practice, that suggests a useful distinction. Losing the anxious inner critic who worries about correct form is one thing. Losing the bodily sense of where your limbs are, or of where the wall is, is another. The first may free movement. The second is a hazard. Chapter 9 offers experiments that let you notice which one is happening.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“Reduced self-referential concern about ‘correct form’ allowing freer exploration.” This matches the measured phenomenon of ego dissolution and the quieting of self-referential brain networks. No study has tested whether it frees movement in martial practice.

What Psilocybin Does to the Moving Body

Chapter 4

Proprioceptive refinement: Heightened sensitivity to helical twisting through the torso and limbs. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

The source document speaks of “heightened sensitivity” in the altered state. I call the experience “mindbending.” Both describe the felt side of practice. This chapter describes the measured side: what controlled studies have found when people under psilocybin are asked to keep time, pay attention, balance, move quickly, or notice touch.

The short version is that psilocybin makes the inner experience of the body richer and stranger, while making most measured kinds of performance somewhat worse. That combination is exactly why an altered session can feel profound and still be the wrong time for a steel dummy or a live blade.

Time stretches, and timing slips

The first systematic study of time under psilocybin tested twelve healthy volunteers on a placebo and two active doses. Psilocybin significantly impaired their ability to reproduce intervals longer than about 2.5 seconds and to synchronize with beats spaced more than 2 seconds apart, and it made their preferred tapping rate slower. These changes came with working-memory deficits and reports of disturbed “time sense,” depersonalization, and derealization. The authors concluded that the serotonin system seems to be selectively involved in processing durations longer than 2 to 3 seconds, and in “the voluntary control of the speed of movement” (Wittmann et al., 2007).

Two details matter for martial practice. First, the longer rhythms that were disrupted are the rhythms of forms, circle walking, and juggling cycles. Second, the study did not test the very fast, reactive timing of a strike, a parry, or a catch, so we simply do not know how that is affected. The absence of measurement is not reassurance.

Attention, memory, and psychomotor speed

In a dose-effect study with eight healthy volunteers, the two larger doses tested reduced performance on a standard attention test by about half compared with placebo (Hasler et al., 2004).

In a larger double-blind study, twenty experienced hallucinogen users completed a battery of tests at several doses. Global cognitive impairment, of the kind seen in delirium, did not occur. But psilocybin produced “orderly and dose-dependent effects” on psychomotor performance, working memory, episodic memory, associative learning, and visual perception (Barrett et al., 2018). In the same participants, psilocybin increased blood pressure and heart rate and “decreased psychomotor performance and balance” (Carbonaro et al., 2018).

A systematic review of 43 papers on the cognitive effects of psychedelics in healthy people found that most reported detrimental or neutral effects on cognition at the peak of the drug’s effect. The authors also noted that small samples and inconsistent methods prevent firm conclusions (Velit-Salazar et al., 2024).

● Evidence: well-established

Psilocybin impairs timing, attention, psychomotor performance, and balance during its peak effects. Controlled laboratory studies consistently find dose-dependent impairment, without global confusion (Wittmann et al., 2007; Hasler et al., 2004; Barrett et al., 2018; Carbonaro et al., 2018; Velit-Salazar et al., 2024).

Touch and the bodily self

The body’s own signals change too. In a combined EEG and fMRI study, psilocybin reduced the brain’s response to surprising touch, in frontal regions, the visual cortex, and the cerebellum. It also reduced an electrical signal of tactile mismatch, and this reduction was associated with altered body- and self-experience. The authors describe this as “aberrant prediction error processing” of touch (Duerler et al., 2021). A review of psychedelics and the bodily self proposes that they alter the predictive processes by which the brain integrates signals from the senses into a coherent sense of the body (Ho et al., 2020).

Put simply, the brain normally predicts what touch will feel like and notices when a prediction is wrong. Under psilocybin, that noticing is altered. For a practitioner, this may be part of why the familiar feel of a bag, a dummy arm, or a partner’s wrist can seem new. It is also a reason to keep contact light. A brain that is less able to register surprising touch is less able to register the early warning signs of an impact going wrong.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Psilocybin changes how touch and the bodily self are processed. A single imaging study found altered processing of surprising touch, linked to changes in body- and self-experience (Duerler et al., 2021). The broader predictive-coding account of the bodily self is a theoretical proposal (Ho et al., 2020).

The heart and the heat

Psilocybin has modest effects on the cardiovascular system. In a pooled analysis of 85 healthy participants, it raised blood pressure and heart rate only moderately; heart rate exceeded 100 beats per minute in 7% of administrations, and a raised body temperature was more common at higher doses. No serious adverse reactions occurred (Straumann et al., 2024). In a direct comparison with LSD, psilocybin raised blood pressure more (Holze et al., 2022). An earlier study found blood pressure moderately elevated about an hour after the highest dose only, with no changes in the electrocardiogram (Hasler et al., 2004).

These are small effects for a healthy person resting in a laboratory. Vigorous exercise adds its own rise in heart rate, blood pressure, and body heat. No study has measured what happens when the two are combined, which is one more reason the practices in Part II are slow, light, and unhurried.

What has never been measured

To be clear about the gaps, here are some things no published study has measured:

  • reaction time to an incoming strike or a thrown object under psilocybin;
  • accuracy of a strike, a weapon cut, or a juggling catch under psilocybin;
  • injury rates in any kind of physical training under psilocybin;
  • whether practising a skill under psilocybin improves, harms, or does not affect that skill when sober.

A review of psychedelics in sport concluded that their effects on athletic performance “remain largely unknown” (Portes et al., 2025). A brief report from 1966 described “time contraction and psychomotor performance” under psilocybin (Fischer & Mead, 1966), but modern research has not taken up skilled movement.

Why this matters

The research gives a coherent picture. Under psilocybin, perception is vivid, meaning is amplified, the self-critic may quiet, and the body may feel newly available. At the same time, longer timing is disrupted, attention is reduced, psychomotor performance and balance are worse, and the processing of surprising touch is altered.

For slow, solo, light practice, these changes are part of what makes the experience worth studying. For fast, forceful, or partnered practice, the same changes are a recipe for injury. The safety section of the source document draws that line plainly: “Do not practice sparring, weapons work, or high-risk movements while in any altered state.” The next chapter explains how to honour that line while still practising curiously.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“It is mindbending.” My experience of training under psilocybin matches what the laboratory research would predict about perception: vivid, strange, and absorbing. The research does not tell us what that experience teaches, or whether it transfers to sober skill.

Part II · Practising Altered

Curiosity is the practice. Care is what makes it possible.

What “Responsibly” Means

Chapter 5

Practice everything altered responsibly. — Cory Snell

The word “responsibly” carries the weight of this whole Part. It is not a disclaimer tacked onto the end of an adventure. It is the set of conditions under which curious, altered practice becomes a way of learning rather than a way of getting hurt.

Research gives a surprisingly clear picture of what those conditions are. Clinical trials of psilocybin are, among other things, decades of careful experiment in making a powerful experience safe. Large surveys of people who use psilocybin on their own describe what goes wrong when those conditions are missing. This chapter turns both into five commitments: know the law, screen yourself honestly, never practise alone, prepare the space, and choose the right tools.

The law, briefly

Psilocybin is a controlled substance in most of the world. In the United States it remains in the most restrictive federal schedule, and in most countries possession is a criminal offence. A few places have created narrow legal frameworks. Two US states, Oregon and Colorado, have voter-approved systems of licensed, supervised psilocybin services; since 2023 Australia has allowed specially authorized psychiatrists to prescribe it for a small number of conditions; and some cities have deprioritized enforcement. These frameworks are specific, regulated, and changing. This book gives no legal advice. Learn the law where you are, and accept the consequences of what you choose.

Screen yourself honestly

The safety guidelines that shaped modern psilocybin research name the main risks plainly. The most likely one is “overwhelming distress during drug action (‘bad trip’), which could lead to potentially dangerous behaviour.” Prolonged psychoses triggered by hallucinogens are less common. The guidelines exclude people with a personal or family history of psychotic disorders or other severe psychiatric disorders (Johnson et al., 2008). Several specific risks deserve attention.

Psychosis and bipolar disorder. In a survey representative of the US adult population, lifetime psychedelic use was not associated overall with recent psychotic symptoms. But there was an interaction with family history: psychotic symptoms were highest among people who had used psychedelics and had a family history of psychotic or bipolar disorders (Simonsson et al., 2025). Clinical trials have excluded people with bipolar disorder, so the risk in that group is largely unstudied.

Lithium. An analysis of online experience reports found that 47% of 62 reports of a classic psychedelic taken with lithium described seizures, and 39% involved medical attention. None of 34 reports with the mood stabilizer lamotrigine did. The authors provisionally concluded that psychedelic use “may pose a significant seizure risk for patients on lithium” (Nayak et al., 2021). Other psychiatric medicines can also interact; discuss any medication with a doctor.

Heart and blood pressure. Psilocybin raises blood pressure and heart rate modestly in healthy people (Hasler et al., 2004; Holze et al., 2022; Straumann et al., 2024). People with heart disease or uncontrolled high blood pressure have generally been excluded from trials.

Persisting perceptual changes. Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD), in which visual disturbances recur long after the drug has worn off, appears to be “a genuine but uncommon disorder,” sometimes lasting months or years, though the data on it are limited (Halpern & Pope, 2003). A scoping review calls it “uncommon yet serious” (Doyle et al., 2022). In the US population survey, 1.3% of people who had used psychedelics reported having been told by a medical professional that they had HPPD (Simonsson et al., 2025).

In clinical trials. A 2024 meta-analysis of studies with 3,504 participants found no serious adverse events among healthy participants. Among participants with existing neuropsychiatric disorders, about 4% had serious adverse events, including worsening depression, suicidal behaviour, psychosis, and convulsive episodes (Hinkle et al., 2024). In a large trial in treatment-resistant depression, adverse events such as headache, nausea, and dizziness occurred in 77% of participants, and suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group (Goodwin et al., 2022).

● Evidence: well-established

Psilocybin is physiologically low in toxicity, but it has specific psychiatric and medical risks. Risks are greater with a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder, with lithium, and in people with existing psychiatric illness. HPPD is uncommon but real (Johnson et al., 2008; Halpern & Pope, 2003; Nayak et al., 2021; Hinkle et al., 2024; Simonsson et al., 2025).

⚠ Caution

Do not practise altered if any of these apply: a personal or family history of psychosis, schizophrenia, or bipolar disorder; taking lithium; heart disease, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or a history of seizures; pregnancy; a current mental health crisis; or taking other psychiatric medication without having discussed it with a doctor. This list is not complete. It is not medical advice. If you are unsure, the answer is no.

Never practise alone

In clinical trials, psilocybin sessions are attended by at least two trained monitors who have built trust with the volunteer beforehand (Johnson et al., 2008). Outside the laboratory, the difference that support makes is visible in the data.

In a survey of 1,993 people describing their single most difficult psilocybin experience, 11% said they had put themselves or others at risk of physical harm, 2.6% had behaved aggressively or violently, and 2.7% had received medical help. The factors that increased the risk of harm included the estimated dose, how long and how difficult the experience was, and the absence of physical comfort and social support (Carbonaro et al., 2016). In a global survey of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year, 0.2% had sought emergency medical treatment; the most common reasons given were poor mindset, poor setting, and mixing substances (Kopra et al., 2022).

For a practitioner, the lesson is direct. A sober, experienced, trusted sitter is the single most important piece of safety equipment in an altered session. Their job is not to coach. It is to keep the space safe, to notice when something is going wrong before you do, to stop the session if needed, and to be a calm human presence if fear arrives.

● Evidence: well-established

Support and setting reduce harm. Laboratory safety guidelines require trained monitors and a safe environment (Johnson et al., 2008). In naturalistic surveys, the absence of comfort and social support, poor setting, and mixing substances are linked to harm and emergency visits (Carbonaro et al., 2016; Kopra et al., 2022).

Set and setting

“Set” is the mindset you bring; “setting” is the physical and social environment. The idea has a long history in psychedelic research, and it has been compared with placebo theory: both hold that expectations, preparation, and beliefs shape the response to a drug (Hartogsohn, 2016). A prospective study of people planning their own psychedelic experiences found that having “clear intentions” was conducive to mystical-type experiences, while a positive set decreased the likelihood of a challenging experience. Baseline personality traits had the strongest effect on later changes in wellbeing (Haijen et al., 2018).

For a practice session, set means arriving rested, unhurried, and emotionally steady, with a simple, curious intention: today I want to watch how my weight moves in the circle walk, or today I want to feel where the spiral starts. Setting means a familiar, private, warm, uncluttered space.

A safe space for altered practice

  • A sober, experienced sitter is present for the whole session and has agreed to stop it if needed.
  • The floor is open, flat, and non-slip, with soft surfaces nearby. No glass, sharp corners, stairs, or open water.
  • Heavy implements, live weapons, and steel or rigid training equipment have been put away or locked out of reach beforehand.
  • No driving, cycling, cooking, or other hazardous tasks for the rest of the day.
  • Water, warm clothing, and a comfortable place to sit or lie down are close at hand.
  • No mixing with alcohol or other drugs.
  • A phone is available to the sitter for emergencies.
  • Either of you can end the movement part of the session at any time, for any reason, without discussion.

Choose the right tools

My own testimony includes practice with weapons, heavy implements, bagwork, and dummy training under psilocybin. This book respects that history and does not lecture about it. It does, however, draw one firm line, and the line comes from the research in Chapter 4.

Psilocybin measurably slows the voluntary speed of movement and disrupts longer timing (Wittmann et al., 2007), reduces attention (Hasler et al., 2004), impairs psychomotor performance (Barrett et al., 2018) and balance (Carbonaro et al., 2018), and alters the processing of surprising touch (Duerler et al., 2021). Every one of those changes matters more as the mass, speed, and hardness of what you are handling increases.

A 6 lb iron ball dropped from a juggling arc is not a soft ball. A 25 lb bar swinging in a ring is not a stick. A steel-armed dummy meets a misjudged strike with steel. A live blade does not forgive a slipped grip. And a sparring partner is another person whose safety depends on your timing and restraint. The source document draws the same line: “Do not practice sparring, weapons work, or high-risk movements while in any altered state.”

Tools for sober practice and for altered sessions.
Sober practice Altered session substitute Why
Iron or steel balls (e.g. 6 lb) Soft juggling balls, beanbags, or a single soft ball Dropped weight, impact on feet and hands
Heavy bar or ring (e.g. 25 lb) A light wooden or bamboo stick, or empty hands Momentum is hard to stop when timing slips
Steel-armed or rigid dummy at force Light touch and slow tracing only, on a padded or wooden dummy Altered touch processing, impact injury
Heavy bag at power Light touch, pushing, leaning, slow contact Wrist and hand injury when alignment drifts
Live or sharp weapons Foam or rubber trainers, or light sticks Cuts and punctures
Partner sparring or fast drills Slow solo flow, shadow work Another person’s safety

⚠ Caution

The line. In an altered session: no sparring or partner drills at speed, no live or sharp weapons, no heavy implements, no forceful striking of the bag or dummy, no inversions, jumps, or high-risk movements, and no training near hazards. Keep all of these for sober practice.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Why this line is a judgement, not a measurement. No study has measured injury rates in any kind of training under psilocybin. The line is my judgement, drawn from what controlled studies show about timing, attention, balance, and touch, and from the source document’s own safety boundaries.

If things get hard

Challenging experiences are common. Even among screened laboratory volunteers, anxiety and fear occur at high doses (Griffiths et al., 2011). When fear, confusion, or panic arrives during a practice session, the movement part of the session is over. Sit or lie down. Let the sitter take care of the space. Slow breathing, a blanket, a hand to hold, quiet music, and the reminder that this state is temporary are all forms of the interpersonal support that, in the laboratory, was enough to manage acute reactions (Studerus et al., 2011). If someone is in danger or medical symptoms appear, call emergency services.

Difficult experiences are not always wasted. In the survey of challenging experiences, 84% of respondents said they had benefited from them (Carbonaro et al., 2016). But that benefit came after the fact. In the moment, the only job is safety.

Slow Forms, Circle Walking, and Tracing Spirals

Chapter 6

Slow, mindful solo work deliberately tracing felt geometric pathways (spirals, circles, continuous arcs) with minimal muscular effort. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Slow practice is the natural home of altered exploration. It asks little of fast timing, which psilocybin disrupts. It keeps the body close to its own centre of balance, which psilocybin makes less reliable. And it leaves room for the thing the altered state seems to offer most: a vivid, unusual, absorbing attention to what the body is actually doing.

This chapter offers explorations, not instructions. Every practice suggested here is untested. The point is curiosity: to notice, to compare, and to record, so that what you find can later be checked.

Why slow?

The research on Tai Chi gives some grounds for thinking slow, attentive movement trains the body’s sense of itself. Long-term practitioners show better joint position sense at the knee (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003) and detect smaller movements at the ankle (Xu et al., 2004). A review of movement-based contemplative practices notes that the cultivation of interoceptive, proprioceptive, and kinesthetic awareness is said to lie at the core of practices such as yoga, qigong, and Tai Chi (Schmalzl et al., 2014). None of these studies involved psilocybin. They describe what slow, attentive practice does on its own.

There is also a reason in the physics of movement. The nervous system tends to plan movements to be as smooth as possible (Flash & Hogan, 1985), and when people draw curves, their speed falls where the curve tightens, following lawful relationships between speed and curvature (Huh & Sejnowski, 2015). Slow practice makes that lawfulness easier to feel. You can notice the hand slowing into the tight part of a spiral and lengthening out along the wide part.

● Evidence: well-established

Slow, attentive movement practice is associated with better body awareness. Long-term Tai Chi practitioners show better proprioception (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003; Xu et al., 2004). Curved movements follow lawful, smooth patterns (Flash & Hogan, 1985; Huh & Sejnowski, 2015).

Before you begin: a sober baseline

The most useful thing you can do for an altered session happens days before it. Film yourself, sober, doing exactly the forms you plan to explore: one slow form, one minute of circle walking, one set of spiral tracings. Note in a journal how each felt. This baseline is what you will compare against later (Chapter 12). Without it, you will have only memory, and memories of altered sessions are shaped by the same meaning-enhancement that colours the session itself (Hartogsohn, 2018).

Exploration 1: The slow form

Choose a short form or sequence you know well, so well that it runs without thought. Perform it once at your usual pace, then again at half that pace, then again more slowly still.

What to notice:

  • Where each turn begins. Does the rotation start at the foot, the hip, the waist, or the hand? Does it feel different from how you have been taught it begins?
  • Weight transfer. Where exactly is the weight at each moment? Can you feel the instant it passes the midpoint between the feet?
  • Resets. The source document describes “micro-adjustments that reduce unnecessary resets.” Where does the form stop and restart rather than flowing? Those are worth noting, not fixing.
  • The inner critic. Is the voice that checks “correct form” quieter, louder, or absent? What does the movement do when it falls silent?
  • Time. Ask your sitter to time the form with a stopwatch, without telling you the result. Afterwards, guess how long it took. Psilocybin disturbs the reproduction of longer intervals (Wittmann et al., 2007), so the difference between your guess and the stopwatch is a small, safe measurement of your own altered time sense.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

The slow form as a mirror. The suggestion that a slow form, performed altered, reveals where turns begin and where resets hide is practitioner experience. Nobody has tested it. The time-estimation exercise draws on a measured effect (Wittmann et al., 2007), but its use in practice is my suggestion.

Exploration 2: Circle walking

Baguazhang’s circle walk is a meditation on a central axis. The source document describes “circle walking and continuous spiraling palm changes,” with “constant transformation and connection to a central axis.” In sober practice, Baguazhang circle walking is a moderate-intensity exercise (Cao & Zhang, 2026).

In an altered session, walk a wide circle, slowly, around a soft marker such as a cushion on the floor, with your sitter outside the circle. Walk in one direction for a short while, then stop completely, stand, and breathe before reversing.

What to notice:

  • The centre. Does attention to the marker hold you on the circle, or does the circle drift? Does the axis feel like it is in the marker, in your own spine, or somewhere between?
  • The feet. How does the outer foot place itself compared with the inner? Is there a rhythm that wants to settle?
  • The palms. If you make a palm change, move very slowly and keep your feet still while you do it. What does the turn feel like from the inside?
  • The visual field. Does the room seem to rotate, stream, or form patterns? Psilocybin’s visual effects can include movement and spiral or tunnel-like forms (Carbonaro et al., 2018; Bressloff et al., 2001). Notice whether these patterns follow your motion, or arise on their own.

⚠ Caution

Dizziness and balance. Walking in circles challenges balance even when sober, and psilocybin impairs balance (Carbonaro et al., 2018). Keep the circle wide and the pace slow. Change direction only after a full stop. If the room starts to spin or your footing feels uncertain, stop, sit down, and let the session become a sitting one.

Exploration 3: Tracing spirals

The simplest geometric practice needs no space at all. Stand or sit comfortably, and with one hand, slowly trace a spiral in the air in front of you, starting small and widening, then narrowing again. Then try a figure-eight. Then try both hands at once, mirroring or opposing.

What to notice:

  • Speed and curvature. Does the hand slow where the curve tightens? Can you feel the arm, shoulder, and torso joining in as the spiral widens? This is the source document’s “small circular deflections scale into whole-body spirals.”
  • The helix in the forearm. The source document describes “heightened sensitivity to helical twisting through the torso and limbs.” As the hand traces, can you feel the forearm rotate? Where does that rotation travel next?
  • Seen versus felt. Close your eyes and trace. Open them and trace. Is the spiral you feel the same as the one you see? Some of the geometry of an altered visual field comes from the visual cortex itself (Bressloff et al., 2001). The felt spiral, traced with eyes closed, is less likely to be borrowed from it.
  • Effort. The source document recommends “minimal muscular effort.” What is the least effort that still produces a clean spiral?

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Seen and felt spirals. The suggestion to compare eyes-open and eyes-closed tracing comes from me. It rests on a real finding, that geometric hallucinations reflect visual cortex architecture (Bressloff et al., 2001), but the exercise itself is untested.

Attention inside and out

Research on attention in movement offers one more thing to explore. In sober practice, directing attention to the effect of a movement, rather than to the body parts making it, generally improves performance and learning (Wulf, 2013) and produces more fluent, automatic movement (Kal et al., 2013).

In an altered session, try both deliberately. For one spiral, attend to the path of the fingertip through space. For the next, attend to the feeling in the elbow and shoulder. Notice which feels smoother, which feels stranger, and which you would want to film. Then, in a sober session afterwards, try both again.

Mostly stillness

Nothing in this chapter needs to fill a session. You may find that a few minutes of tracing, one slow form, or a single wide circle is more than enough to study, and that most of an altered experience is better spent sitting, resting, and letting it pass. Speak or record a few words about what you noticed while it is fresh, and let the movement end long before the experience does.

⚠ Caution

Stop if any of these appear: dizziness or loss of balance; fear, confusion, or a sense of losing touch with where you are; chest pain, a racing heart, or breathlessness; or your sitter asks you to stop. The session becomes a sitting one.

Free Form, Shadow Work, and the Soft Ball

Chapter 7

Emphasis on continuous, non-repetitive chaining rather than discrete, reset-based technique. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Slow forms are a way of looking closely at known movement. Free form is a way of discovering movement you did not know you had. The source document describes “continuous kinetic chaining and flow states that escape rigid, linear technique sequences.” I list free form and juggling among the practices he has explored altered. This chapter looks at three kinds of open, exploratory practice: free movement, shadow work, and light juggling with soft balls.

Free form

Free form means movement without a set sequence: one motion growing out of the last, following whatever path the body finds. In sober practice it is a way of training adaptability. The source document’s phrase “continuous, non-repetitive chaining” captures the aim: no stops, no resets, no repeated drill, just one unbroken line of motion.

Free movement connects to research on flow, the absorbed state in which action seems to happen effortlessly. Research on flow in sport has grown substantially (Swann et al., 2012). An attentional account proposes that flow involves effortless attention, reduced self-referential thinking, and efficient, automatic control of action (Harris et al., 2017). Reduced self-referential thinking is also, as Chapter 3 described, one of the measured features of the psilocybin state (Carhart-Harris et al., 2012; Lebedev et al., 2015). Whether the two states resemble each other in movement has never been studied.

What to notice in free form:

  • Where the movement wants to go. Begin with a single slow spiral of the hands and let it lead. What does the body do next if you do not decide?
  • Chains and breaks. Where does the chain break into a pause or a reset? Is the break physical (loss of balance), mental (a decision), or emotional (a flicker of self-consciousness)?
  • Familiar fragments. Do pieces of known forms appear unbidden? Which ones? Practised sequences are stored as chunks (Sakai et al., 2003), and a free movement that keeps returning to the same chunk is telling you something about your own repertoire.
  • The edge of balance. Free movement drifts toward the limits of balance. Psilocybin impairs balance (Carbonaro et al., 2018). When you feel the edge, come back to centre.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Flow is a measurable state with features that overlap with the psychedelic state. Both involve reduced self-referential thinking (Harris et al., 2017; Carhart-Harris et al., 2012). No study has compared them directly, or examined flow in movement under psilocybin.

Shadow work

Shadow work is fighting an imagined opponent: striking, evading, and moving as if someone were there. It is one of the oldest solo practices in every combat tradition, and it has a scientific cousin in research on mental practice and motor imagery. A meta-analysis of 303 imaging experiments found that imagining movement recruits brain networks that overlap with those used in watching and performing it (Hardwick et al., 2018), and meta-analyses of behavioural studies find small but reliable benefits of mental practice on performance (Driskell et al., 1994; Toth et al., 2020).

In an altered session, shadow work becomes something stranger. The imagined opponent may feel vivid. The space may seem to contain lines, arcs, and geometries. And because psilocybin amplifies perceived meaning (Preller et al., 2017; Hartogsohn, 2018), each imagined exchange can feel deeply significant.

What to explore:

  • Slow shadow. Move at a fraction of normal speed. Imagine the opponent’s arm arriving, and trace your redirection as a spiral. Notice whether the geometry you feel matches what you have been taught.
  • The imagined partner’s centre. Where do you imagine the opponent’s balance to be? How does your movement relate to it?
  • Emotional weather. Shadow work under psilocybin can bring up feelings: aggression, fear, grief, or joy. Notice them, without acting them out. If fear or anger grows, stop and sit.
  • Distance. Keep strikes well short of walls, furniture, and your sitter. Under altered perception, distance is easy to misjudge.

⚠ Caution

Slow and empty-handed. Shadow work in an altered session should be slow, unarmed or with a foam trainer, and performed in open space well away from walls, furniture, and other people. No full-speed strikes, no kicks above waist height, no spins or jumps. Imagined opponents should stay imagined; never shadow toward a real person.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Shadow work as a window into one’s own fighting mind. That altered shadow work reveals one’s habitual patterns, fears, and geometries is practitioner experience. Mental practice in general is supported (Driskell et al., 1994; Toth et al., 2020), but altered shadow work has never been studied.

Light juggling with soft balls

Juggling is one of the best-studied skills in motor neuroscience. When adults learned a three-ball cascade over three months, grey matter expanded transiently in a region specialized for perceiving visual motion and in a region linking vision to action; the expansion decreased once practice stopped (Draganski et al., 2004). Expert jugglers show higher grey matter density in visual-motion regions, correlated with their performance (Gerber et al., 2014). Skilled cascade juggling relies on flexibly coupled timing between the two hands and the balls, not a rigid metronome (Beek & Turvey, 1992). The cascade itself traces a sideways figure-eight in the air.

For an altered session, the right tool is the one the science used: ordinary soft juggling balls or beanbags. A dropped soft ball bounces off a foot harmlessly. The heavy iron balls described in Book 1 do not.

What to explore:

  • One ball. Toss one ball from hand to hand in a low arc. Watch the arc. Does it look like a curve, a sequence of positions, a trail, or a pattern? Psilocybin can bring textured, kaleidoscopic, and moving visual effects (Carbonaro et al., 2018). Which part of what you see is the ball, and which part is the seeing?
  • The rhythm. Juggling rhythms are longer cycles, and psilocybin disrupts the reproduction and synchronization of longer intervals (Wittmann et al., 2007). Does the rhythm feel faster, slower, or stretched? Ask your sitter to film a short clip so you can compare its tempo with your sober baseline.
  • The figure-eight. If you can cascade, do so slowly and low. Can you feel the figure-eight being drawn by the hands, or only see it in the balls?
  • The drop. Notice what happens when a ball falls. Does self-criticism arrive? Does it matter? The quieting of self-referential concern that the source document describes may show up here first.

● Evidence: well-established

Juggling ordinary balls is a well-studied skill. Learning it produces measurable, partly transient changes in brain regions for visual motion (Draganski et al., 2004; Gerber et al., 2014), and skilled juggling depends on flexible timing between the hands (Beek & Turvey, 1992). No study has examined juggling under psilocybin.

Expect to perform worse

It is worth saying plainly: if you juggle, shadow, or move freely under psilocybin, you should expect to perform less well than when sober. Psychomotor performance, working memory, and visual perception are all impaired in a dose-dependent way (Barrett et al., 2018). Juggling will probably drop more balls. Free form will probably wobble more.

That is not a failure. The purpose of an altered session, in my philosophy, is not performance but understanding: “to bring curiosity to practice while altered.” A dropped ball, a wobble, a broken chain are data. They are what the changed nervous system does. Noticing them with interest rather than frustration may be the most valuable thing the session teaches.

Touch: The Bag, the Dummy, and the Listening Hand

Chapter 8

Partner work oriented toward listening, blending, and following natural lines of force rather than imposing sequences. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Touch is where martial practice becomes most honest. A bag, a dummy, or a partner’s arm tells you immediately whether your alignment is true, whether your weight is behind your hand, and whether your timing was early or late. I include bagwork and dummy training among the practices I have explored under psilocybin.

This chapter brings together what research says about contact training: the wooden dummy, Wing Chun, conditioning of the forearm and hand, push hands, and the role of touch in learning. It is, frankly, a thin literature. It then describes how to explore touch, lightly, in an altered session.

The wooden dummy: what is known

The wooden dummy, or mook yan jong, is a post with protruding arms and a leg, used in Wing Chun and related arts to rehearse contact, angles, footwork, and transitions against a fixed structure. Practitioners describe its value in terms of contact feedback: the arms rebound and redirect, the trunk sets the distance, and the angles teach the practitioner where their own centreline is.

There are no published scientific studies of wooden dummy training. A search of PubMed at the time of writing found none on the mook yan jong, on dummy training in any martial art, on contact rebound, or on the sensitivity that dummy work is said to build. The broader research on Wing Chun consists of a handful of papers: an early physiological study showing that Wing Chun exercise is more demanding than Tai Chi (Schneider & Leung, 1991), a small motion-capture study of punching sequences in four experienced practitioners (Fuchs et al., 2017), and an essay proposing a framework for wellbeing through Wing Chun’s principles (Watson & Kemp, 2025).

What follows are the nearest scientific neighbours to dummy work. None of them studied a dummy.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Dummy training has no direct research base. No study has examined the mook yan jong or similar apparatus. Wing Chun itself has been studied only in a few small physiological and biomechanical papers (Schneider & Leung, 1991; Fuchs et al., 2017).

Forearm and bone: the conditioning question

Dummy work, like much traditional training, involves repeated contact between the forearms and a hard surface. Practitioners often describe the forearms as becoming “conditioned.” What can be said about this?

Bone responds to loading. Studies of racquet and throwing athletes show that their loaded arms develop larger and stronger bones than their non-loaded arms, with changes in shape and size as well as density (Bass et al., 2002; Warden et al., 2014). In a one-year study of previously inactive young men, those who took part in recreational Kung Fu twice a week increased bone mineral density in the forearm and radius, along with strength and fitness, while a control group did not (Khalil et al., 2023). That study did not involve dummy work specifically, and its groups were not described as randomized.

Bone needs rest. In a classic study in rats, the same daily number of loading cycles built stronger bone when split into four short bouts separated by hours than when given all at once (Robling et al., 2002). Bone cells desensitize to repeated loading and need time to recover their sensitivity, which suggests that exercise for bone should use brief, dynamic sessions with rest between them (Turner & Robling, 2003).

Hard conditioning has costs. An early medical report on serious karate hand-conditioners described a technique of building callus over deliberately damaged tissue and concluded that serious hand conditioning was unnecessary and “not recommended” (Larose & Sik, 1969). Hand and wrist injuries are common in the striking arts, and protection and good technique reduce the risk (Diesselhorst et al., 2013; Drury et al., 2017).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Martial arts loading can strengthen forearm bone, but dummy conditioning is untested. Recreational Kung Fu increased forearm bone density in one non-randomized study (Khalil et al., 2023), consistent with what is known about bone and loading (Bass et al., 2002; Warden et al., 2014). Whether dummy contact conditions bone or soft tissue, and how much is too much, has not been studied.

The listening hand: push hands and contact sensitivity

The closest the research comes to “contact sensitivity” is a handful of studies of Tai Chi push hands.

Force-plate studies show that push hands is, mechanically, a gentle practice. In ten practitioners, the total force under both feet stayed almost exactly equal to body weight through every phase of attack and defence, which the authors interpret as meaning that practitioners “do not push or resist their opponents” in the ordinary sense (Chang et al., 2014). In another group of ten, vertical foot forces during push hands were lower than in walking or Tai Chi gait (Wong et al., 2013). In the single-case study described in Chapter 2, an experienced master neutralized pushes with subtle postural adjustments that shifted the incoming force to the rear leg, while inexperienced people lost their balance (Chen et al., 2010). And when long-term push hands practitioners were suddenly released from a horizontal load, they responded with smaller vertical force spikes and slower backward knee movement than controls, suggesting better reactive postural control (Sever et al., 2021).

Together, these studies support a modest version of the “listening” idea. Skilled practitioners deal with incoming force by adjusting posture and redirecting it into the ground, rather than meeting it with muscle. None of them measured touch sensitivity directly.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Push hands is low-force and associated with good reactive balance. Small force-plate studies show near-body-weight ground forces and quieter responses to perturbation in experienced practitioners (Wong et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2014; Sever et al., 2021), and a single case shows skilled redirection (Chen et al., 2010).

Touch as a teacher

Motor learning research offers one more relevant idea. Feedback added to a movement, from a coach’s voice, a visual display, or a physical device, can enhance learning, and recent technology has made it possible to study touch-based (haptic) feedback as well as visual and auditory feedback in complex, realistic tasks (Sigrist et al., 2013). A dummy or a bag gives the practitioner a kind of natural haptic feedback with every contact: the arm moves or it does not; the bag swings straight or it twists.

Under psilocybin, that feedback channel itself changes. In the imaging study described in Chapter 4, psilocybin reduced the brain’s response to surprising touch, and the reduction was associated with altered body- and self-experience (Duerler et al., 2021). Familiar contact may feel new. Contact that should feel wrong, the early twinge of a misaligned wrist, may be noticed less.

Exploring touch, lightly

These are explorations for an altered session. They are deliberately light. The point is to feel, not to hit.

The bag.

  • Stand close to a heavy bag and place both palms on it. Lean gently into it, then let it push you back. Where in your body do you feel the push arrive?
  • Push the bag slowly with one palm and follow it as it swings away and returns. Can you meet the return without bracing, the way push hands practitioners meet force by redirecting it?
  • Touch the bag with the forearm and slowly roll the forearm across its surface. Notice the spiral in the forearm described in Chapter 6.

The dummy.

  • With your hands resting lightly on the dummy’s arms, trace slowly around them: over, under, and between. Feel the angles.
  • Move slowly through a familiar sequence of positions with contact so light it would not dent a piece of paper. Notice where your centreline is relative to the dummy’s trunk.
  • Close your eyes, keep one hand on a dummy arm, and slowly step around. Can you feel the structure through one point of contact?

Self-touch.

  • Place one hand on the opposite forearm and slowly rotate the forearm underneath it. Feel the bones turn. This is the “helical twisting” the source document describes, felt from outside.

⚠ Caution
