Touch, not impact. In an altered session, contact with the bag and dummy should be light touch, leaning, pushing, and slow tracing only. No striking at speed or power, no conditioning, no forearm or shin impact, and never work on a steel-armed or rigid dummy. Psilocybin alters the processing of surprising touch (Duerler et al., 2021) and impairs psychomotor performance (Barrett et al., 2018), which removes the early warnings that protect wrists, knuckles, and forearms. Keep forceful contact training for sober sessions.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

What dummy and bag work feel like altered. My testimony includes bagwork and dummy training under psilocybin. What such practice teaches about contact, rebound, and sensitivity has never been studied. The light-touch explorations here are my suggestions.

The Inner Senses: Experiments in Proprioception and Interoception

Chapter 9

This is how you truly understand your mind and body. — Cory Snell

The source document names three channels through which perception may shift: “visual pattern recognition, proprioception, and interoception.” The first is the most dramatic. The other two are quieter and perhaps more useful to a martial artist. Proprioception is the sense of where the body’s parts are and how they are moving. Interoception is the sense of what is happening inside the body: heartbeat, breath, warmth, tension, hunger, the gut.

This chapter describes what is known about these senses, and then offers simple experiments that turn an altered session into something close to a personal laboratory. The experiments are designed to produce small, checkable observations rather than grand insights.

What is known

Proprioception can be trained. Long-term Tai Chi practitioners reposition the knee more accurately than controls (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003) and detect smaller passive ankle movements than sedentary people or long-term swimmers and runners (Xu et al., 2004).

Interoception has several dimensions. The anterior insula has been proposed as a key region for representing the body’s internal state and for subjective feeling (Craig, 2009). Researchers distinguish interoceptive accuracy, measured by objective tests such as detecting one’s own heartbeat; interoceptive sensibility, how good people believe they are; and interoceptive awareness, how well their confidence tracks their actual accuracy. In a sample of 80 people, these three dimensions were distinct, and accuracy was only partly predicted by the other two (Garfinkel et al., 2015). In other words, feeling that you are in touch with your body is not the same as being in touch with it.

Contemplative practice may change how bodily signals are interpreted. A review of interoception and contemplative practice proposes a predictive coding model of mind–body integration, describing a tension between expected and felt sensation, and suggests that contemplative practices may reduce maladaptive interpretations of bodily sensations (Farb et al., 2015).

Psilocybin alters the bodily self. As Chapter 4 described, psilocybin changes how the brain processes surprising touch, in ways linked to altered body- and self-experience (Duerler et al., 2021), and theorists propose that psychedelics alter the predictive processes that build a coherent bodily self (Ho et al., 2020). There appears to be no published controlled study of heartbeat detection or joint position sense under psilocybin.

● Evidence: well-established

Feeling in touch with the body and being accurate about it are different things. Interoceptive accuracy, sensibility, and awareness are distinct and dissociable (Garfinkel et al., 2015). Proprioception is trainable through slow practice such as Tai Chi (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003; Xu et al., 2004).

That distinction is the key to this chapter. The altered state can make bodily sensations feel more vivid. Vividness is a change in sensibility. It may or may not be a change in accuracy. The only way to tell is to test.

Experiments for an altered session

Each experiment below is simple, safe, and produces a small observation that your sitter can record. Do each one sober first, to make a baseline, and again in the altered session. Afterwards, compare. These are informal self-observations, not scientific measurements; Chapter 11 explains their limits.

1. Mirror arms (joint position). Sit comfortably with your eyes closed. Your sitter gently lifts one of your arms to a position and holds it. Without looking, place your other arm in the mirror position. Your sitter photographs both arms. Repeat with three or four positions. Afterwards, compare the photographs from the sober and altered sessions. Did the mirroring become more accurate, less accurate, or about the same?

2. Weight centre. Stand with feet parallel, eyes closed, near a wall or your sitter. Shift your weight slowly toward the toes until you feel it arrive, then toward the heels, then side to side. Say “now” each time you think your weight is exactly centred. Your sitter notes how often your body was visibly upright and still at that moment. This is crude, but it brings attention to the felt centre that circle walking and push hands depend on.

3. Heartbeat counting. Sit quietly. For a period your sitter times, silently count the heartbeats you can feel, without touching your pulse. Your sitter counts your actual pulse at the wrist at the same time. Compare the two counts. Then rate, from one to ten, how confident you were. This is a simplified version of the kind of heartbeat task used in interoception research, and it separates accuracy from confidence (Garfinkel et al., 2015).

4. Breath edges. Breathe naturally and notice the precise moment each inhalation turns into exhalation. Is the turn a point, a pause, or a curve? Some practitioners describe the breath as circular. Does it feel circular now?

5. The spiral inside. Stand still and very slowly rotate the torso a little to one side and back. Where do you feel the twist? In the spine, the hips, the ribs, the belly? Draw it afterwards. The source document describes “heightened sensitivity to helical twisting through the torso and limbs.” Compare your drawing with one made sober.

6. Time. Close your eyes and say “now” when you think one minute has passed. Your sitter notes the actual time. Psilocybin disturbs the reproduction of longer intervals (Wittmann et al., 2007); this gives you a direct, harmless glimpse of how your own time sense has shifted.

7. The self in the body. Lie down. Notice where “you” seem to be located: behind the eyes, in the chest, everywhere, nowhere. Notice whether the boundary between body and floor, or body and room, feels clear. Ego dissolution can include a dissolving of the border between self and world (Lebedev et al., 2015). Notice, without trying to change anything, and record what you can afterwards.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Self-experiments in an altered state. These experiments are my suggestions for turning curiosity into checkable observations. They borrow the logic of research tasks but are not research. Expect your results to be noisy, and do not treat a single session as proof of anything.

⚠ Caution

Stillness is safe; standing is a choice. Most of these experiments can be done sitting or lying down. Experiment 2 involves standing with eyes closed; do it only near a wall or with your sitter’s hands ready, and skip it if balance feels uncertain. Stop any experiment that brings fear, nausea, or confusion.

What the experiments can teach

Two outcomes are especially interesting.

If your accuracy stays the same or worsens while your sense of vividness rises, you have learned something important about the altered state: that its feeling of heightened body awareness may be partly a change in how sensations are experienced rather than in how well they are detected. That is a valuable thing to know before trusting any insight from a session.

If your accuracy genuinely improves on some task, perhaps the mirror arms or the felt spiral, you have something worth following up in sober practice. Can you reproduce the improvement sober, using the same focus of attention? If so, the altered state may have shown you a door that was already there. If not, the improvement may have been noise.

Either way, you will have done what my philosophy asks: studied your own mind and body directly, with curiosity, and written down what you found.

Part III · Pattern

A brain is a machine for finding patterns. It finds the real ones. It also finds the others.

How Brains Find Patterns

Chapter 10

Pattern recognition: Seeing how small circular deflections scale into whole-body spirals or how linear actions integrate into larger enclosing fields. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Pattern finding is at the heart of both martial skill and the psychedelic experience. A skilled fighter sees the shape of an attack before it lands. A skilled internal artist feels the spiral that connects a wrist deflection to a turn of the hips. And people under psilocybin often report that the world, their movement, and their own minds seem full of patterns and connections.

This chapter describes what science knows about how ordinary brains find patterns, and how experts come to see what novices cannot. The next chapter describes how brains find patterns that are not there, and how to tell the difference.

Chunks: the expert’s alphabet

The classic work on expert pattern perception comes from chess. Research beginning in the 1970s proposed the chunking theory of expertise: that experts perceive and remember a position not piece by piece, but as a small number of meaningful groups, or chunks, held in a short-term memory of limited capacity (Chase & Simon, 1973). Later work refined it. When players ranging from club level to grandmaster were shown up to five chess positions in quick succession, experts recalled more pieces than the original theory predicted; one chess master gradually learned to reproduce nine boards, placing as many as 160 pieces correctly. To explain this, the researchers proposed that experts also use larger long-term memory structures, called templates, into which new information can be slotted rapidly (Gobet & Simon, 1996).

A review of chunking across many areas of learning distinguishes two kinds: one “deliberate, under strategic control, and goal-oriented,” and the other “automatic, continuous, and linked to perceptual processes” (Gobet et al., 2001). Movement has chunks too. When people practise sequences of movements, they spontaneously group them into chunks that become units of performance (Sakai et al., 2003).

For a martial artist, this is the scientific version of a familiar experience. A beginner sees an opponent’s arm, shoulder, and step separately. An expert sees a jab coming. The same is true of internal practice: a beginner feels a wrist turn, a hip turn, and a weight shift; an experienced practitioner feels one spiral.

● Evidence: well-established

Experts perceive in chunks and templates. Expert memory and perception depend on learned, meaningful groupings of information, in chess and in many other domains (Chase & Simon, 1973; Gobet & Simon, 1996; Gobet et al., 2001). Practised movement sequences are also chunked (Sakai et al., 2003).

Statistical learning: patterns without trying

The brain also learns patterns automatically, without being told to look. In a famous experiment, eight-month-old infants listened to a continuous stream of nonsense syllables for just two minutes. From that brief exposure, they segmented “words” out of the stream, using nothing but the statistical relationships between neighbouring sounds (Saffran et al., 1996). Adults do the same with vision. People who passively watched scenes of shapes learned, rapidly and automatically, which shapes tended to occur together and in which arrangements. The authors connect this to a theory that the visual system works by detecting “suspicious coincidences” (Fiser & Aslin, 2001).

Perceptual learning, the improvement of sensory abilities with practice, can even happen outside the focus of attention. A unified model proposes that learning occurs when signals from the stimulus coincide in time with diffuse signals related to task performance and reward (Seitz & Watanabe, 2005).

This matters for practice in two ways. First, the patterns you absorb in training are not only the ones you consciously study. Repetitions of a form, a partner’s habits, the rhythm of a bag, all teach the brain their statistics. Second, a brain built to detect “suspicious coincidences” will sometimes find coincidences that mean nothing.

● Evidence: well-established

Brains learn statistical patterns rapidly and automatically. Infants segment words from two minutes of speech (Saffran et al., 1996), adults learn visual co-occurrences passively (Fiser & Aslin, 2001), and perceptual learning can occur outside attention (Seitz & Watanabe, 2005).

Seeing the attack before it comes

Combat sports research shows how pattern perception becomes skill. A meta-analysis found that expert athletes are better than novices at picking up perceptual cues and anticipating what will happen next, using fewer, longer visual fixations (Mann et al., 2007). Karate experts responding to filmed attacks were more accurate at predicting the attack from very early cues, even though their simple reaction times were no faster than novices’ (Mori et al., 2002). In on-mat karate tasks, experts detected a repeated attack pattern after only five repetitions, while novices did not (Milazzo et al., 2016). A motion-capture study of karate sparring found that the defender’s reaction depended on the attacking technique, and that a leading-hand jab was easier to anticipate than a reverse punch or a round kick (Petri et al., 2017).

Expert pattern perception can also transfer. Karate experts were as good as taekwondo experts at anticipating taekwondo techniques, and even performed like domain experts when anticipating skills from Australian football, which near-experts could not. The authors suggest that transfer depends on expertise and an understanding of principles, supplemented by similarities between domains (Rosalie & Müller, 2014).

The best way to study such expertise, researchers argue, is first to capture it with representative tasks in the laboratory, then trace the processes behind it, and then identify the practice that builds it (Williams & Ericsson, 2005).

● Evidence: well-established

Combat expertise is largely perceptual pattern recognition. Experts anticipate from early cues, detect repeated patterns quickly, and can transfer anticipation skill across related domains (Mann et al., 2007; Mori et al., 2002; Milazzo et al., 2016; Rosalie & Müller, 2014).

Geometry as a pattern

The source document’s “pattern recognition” is a specific kind: “seeing how small circular deflections scale into whole-body spirals or how linear actions integrate into larger enclosing fields.” In the language of this chapter, that is the formation of a larger chunk or template: perceiving many movements as one shape.

This is plausible, and it is how expertise generally develops. But it raises the question that drives the next chapter. Real pattern learning in experts comes from many thousands of exposures to real structure, with feedback that tells the learner when they are wrong. An altered session offers something different: a brain whose priors may be relaxed, whose sense of meaning is amplified, and whose visual system is generating geometric patterns of its own (Chapter 3). Patterns found in that state could be real structure, newly noticed. They could also be the brain’s own geometry projected onto the movement.

What altered pattern perception might offer

There is no research on whether psilocybin helps anyone learn movement patterns. There are only hypotheses and testimony.

The REBUS hypothesis proposes that psychedelics relax high-level priors and free bottom-up information (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019). If that is right, a practitioner might perceive their movement with fewer of the expectations that normally filter it, and so notice structure they had overlooked. The ALBUS proposal adds that, in other conditions, priors may become stronger and be imposed on perception, as in pareidolia and apophenia (Safron et al., 2025). Both may happen in the same session.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“Recognition rather than invention.” The source document’s stance is the right one for pattern finding. Treat every pattern seen in an altered session as a hypothesis about movement that already exists, to be recognized and tested sober, not as a new invention to be trusted on the strength of how it felt.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Psychedelics and pattern learning: theory only. REBUS and ALBUS suggest that psychedelics might both loosen and strengthen the brain’s perceptual expectations (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019; Safron et al., 2025). Neither has been tested on movement learning.

False Patterns, and How to Check Them

Chapter 11

Insights require subsequent sober training to become durable. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Every pattern-finding system makes two kinds of mistake. It can miss a pattern that is there. Or it can find one that is not. Psychologists call the second kind of mistake illusory pattern perception. Its everyday forms have names: pareidolia, seeing faces or shapes in random noise, clouds, or toast; and apophenia, perceiving meaningful connections between unrelated things.

A practitioner who explores altered states needs to understand these mistakes better than anyone, because the altered state is, among other things, a state of amplified pattern and amplified meaning. This chapter explains the science and then offers a practical method for checking whether a pattern found in an altered session is real.

Seeing faces in noise

The tendency to see patterns in noise is easy to provoke in ordinary people. In a brain-imaging study titled “Seeing Jesus in toast,” participants viewed images of pure visual noise but were told that half of them contained a face or a letter. They reported seeing faces 34% of the time and letters 38% of the time, even though none were present. When they “saw” a face, the brain’s face-processing region responded. The authors conclude that face processing has “a strong top-down component whereby sensory input with even the slightest suggestion of a face can result in the interpretation of a face” (Liu et al., 2014).

Notice the ingredient that made the illusion work: expectation. The participants were told what to look for, and they found it.

Need, belief, and illusion

The urge to find patterns is not only perceptual; it is also motivational. In six experiments, people who had been made to feel a lack of control were more likely to see images in noise, form illusory correlations in stock market information, perceive conspiracies, and develop superstitions. Affirming their sense of self reduced the effect (Whitson & Galinsky, 2008). In another series of studies, perceiving patterns in random coin tosses and in chaotic paintings predicted belief in conspiracy theories and the supernatural (van Prooijen et al., 2018). A large signal-detection study of 723 people found that paranormal beliefs were linked to a more liberal response bias and lower perceptual sensitivity, driven by false alarms; the associations were modest compared with other sources of variation (Müller & Hartmann, 2023).

Not every chemical push toward pattern does the same thing. In a preregistered double-blind study, a drug that enhances dopamine transmission did not increase illusory pattern perception, though the authors note that the study’s power was limited (Smith et al., 2024).

● Evidence: well-established

Illusory pattern perception is common, and expectation and motivation increase it. Expectation produces pareidolia in noise (Liu et al., 2014); lacking control increases illusory pattern perception (Whitson & Galinsky, 2008); and the tendency predicts unusual beliefs (van Prooijen et al., 2018; Müller & Hartmann, 2023).

Psychedelics and the feeling of significance

Psychedelics push on exactly the levers that produce false patterns. LSD caused volunteers to attribute personal relevance to previously meaningless stimuli (Preller et al., 2017). Psychedelics are thought to enhance the perception of significance in general (Hartogsohn, 2018). Psilocybin’s visual system generates geometry of its own, in the form of lattices, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals (Bressloff et al., 2001; Kometer et al., 2013). And the ALBUS model proposes that psychedelic states can involve “the imposition of prior expectations on perception (e.g. hallucinations and pareidolia)” and delusional thinking, including “apophenia, paranoia, engendering of inaccurate interpretations of events, and potentially false memories” (Safron et al., 2025).

Now put these together with the setting of an altered martial practice session. A practitioner who expects to see spirals in movement, whose visual cortex is generating spirals, and whose sense of meaning is amplified, is primed to find spirals everywhere. Some of them will be real. The feeling of discovery will be equally strong for all of them.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Psychedelics amplify meaning and can promote false pattern perception. LSD increased the attribution of personal relevance to meaningless stimuli (Preller et al., 2017). Theoretical models propose that psychedelics enhance meaning (Hartogsohn, 2018) and can involve pareidolia and apophenia (Safron et al., 2025). Direct tests of illusory pattern perception under psilocybin are lacking.

The insight test

How, then, can you check whether a pattern you found in an altered session is real? The answer is to turn the insight into a prediction about sober movement, and then to test the prediction in a way that does not depend on your own feelings.

Step 1. Write it down as a claim. Not “the spiral was everything,” but something you could be wrong about: When I let the deflection begin at the back foot rather than the hand, the turn is smoother and my head stays level.

Step 2. Make a prediction. If the claim is real, what should be visibly different in a sober performance? Head height should vary less; the form should have fewer visible pauses.

Step 3. Test it sober, several times. Perform the movement sober, with and without the change, several times each, on more than one day. Single trials are noise; measurement scientists recommend multiple trials and warn that learning or fatigue can masquerade as real change (Hopkins, 2000).

Step 4. Film it, and let someone else judge. Film every trial from the same angle. Then ask a trusted training partner to watch the clips without knowing which is which, and to say which looks smoother, more connected, or more balanced. People are often poor judges of their own performance (Kruger & Dunning, 1999), and expectation alone can change performance in sport (Beedie & Foad, 2009). A blind judgement removes both problems.

Step 5. Keep score honestly. Did the blind judge pick the “insight” version more often than chance? Did the predicted measure change? If yes, you may have recognized something real. If not, the insight may have been a beautiful false alarm, and that is worth knowing too.

Signs that a pattern may be illusory

  • It felt overwhelmingly significant but cannot be stated as a specific, testable claim.
  • It explains everything: every movement, every art, every life event.
  • It cannot be reproduced sober, even with effort and time.
  • A blind judge cannot tell the “insight” version from the ordinary one.
  • It came with a sense of special, secret, or exclusive knowledge.
  • It conflicts with basic physics or anatomy, or with what skilled teachers can see.

Recognition, again

The source document’s stance, “recognition rather than invention,” is a natural guard against false patterns. If the geometries are “already latent in efficient movement,” then a real insight should make sober movement measurably more efficient, and an illusory one will not. The document also states the test directly: “Insights require subsequent sober training to become durable.”

The insight test is not a way of dismissing altered experience. It is a way of honouring it. A pattern that survives sober replication and a blind judge is no longer just a feeling. It is knowledge.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

The insight test. This method is my suggestion, built from general principles of measurement and bias (Hopkins, 2000; Kruger & Dunning, 1999; Beedie & Foad, 2009). It is a practical safeguard, not a validated research protocol.

Part IV · Carrying It Home

What you saw in one afternoon becomes yours only in a hundred ordinary ones.

Integration: Journal, Trace, Film, Test

Chapter 12

Any insights gained through temporary perceptual shifts are useful only when deliberately carried into regular practice. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

In psychedelic research, integration means the work done after an experience to make sense of it and carry what was valuable into ordinary life. In this book, integration is a companion to altered practice rather than its goal. The session is where the curiosity happens. Integration is how the curiosity becomes something that lasts.

The source document puts it plainly: “Insights require subsequent sober training to become durable,” and geometric awareness is “a lens for refining existing practice, not a replacement for progressive, disciplined training.” This chapter describes four tools for that work: the journal, sober tracing, filmed comparison, and the insight test from Chapter 11.

Why integration matters

The research on psilocybin’s lasting effects is, in one sense, research on integration. In laboratory studies, volunteers rated their psilocybin sessions as among the most meaningful experiences of their lives months later (Griffiths et al., 2006; Griffiths et al., 2008). In a prospective study of people taking psychedelics on their own initiative, wellbeing increased two weeks afterwards and stayed raised at four weeks (Haijen et al., 2018). But in that same study, baseline traits explained more of the change in wellbeing than anything about the experience itself. What a person brings to the experience, and what they do with it, seems to matter as much as the experience.

For skill, the logic is even simpler. Skill changes through repeated practice over time. Bone adapts over months (Warden et al., 2014). Habits take weeks to months to become automatic (Lally et al., 2010). Grey matter changes associated with learning to juggle faded when practice stopped (Draganski et al., 2004). Whatever an altered session shows you, it will last only if it is practised.

Tool 1: The journal

Write within a day of the session, while memory is fresh, and again a week later. Memories of altered states are shaped by the same meaning-enhancement that colours the experience (Hartogsohn, 2018), so writing early captures more detail, and writing later shows what still seems important.

What to record:

  • Observations. What did you notice in each practice: where the turn started, how the circle felt, what the bag felt like, what happened in each experiment? Be concrete.
  • Measurements. Your sitter’s notes: the stopwatch times, the photographs, the heartbeat counts.
  • Claims. Which observations would you like to test? Write each as a specific claim (Chapter 11).
  • Feelings. What emotions came up? Was there fear, grief, joy, or aggression? Feelings are part of studying the mind.
  • Surprises and difficulties. What went wrong, felt bad, or did not match expectations?

A template is provided in the Appendix.

Tool 2: Sober tracing

In the days after a session, return to the movements you explored, sober, and slowly. The source document describes this as “slow, mindful solo work deliberately tracing felt geometric pathways (spirals, circles, continuous arcs) with minimal muscular effort.”

Try to find, sober, what you felt altered. Trace the spiral. Walk the circle. Lean into the bag. Close your eyes and feel the forearm turn. Sometimes the sensation will be there, fainter but recognizable. Sometimes it will not. Both are information.

Then map what you find onto your existing practice: “mapping observed or felt patterns onto existing forms, bag work, or partner exercises,” in the source document’s words. A spiral that started in the back foot in a tracing exercise can be looked for in the form, then on the bag, and eventually, in sober partner practice, in a push hands exchange.

Tool 3: Filmed comparison

If you filmed a sober baseline before the session (Chapter 6), film the same movements again, sober, a week after the session, and again a month later. Same angle, same distance, same lighting, same clothing if possible.

Then compare. Watch the clips side by side. Better still, ask a training partner to watch them without knowing which is which (Chapter 11). Look for specific, visible things: head height, pauses, the line of the spine, the path of the hand, the timing of the feet. A filmed comparison protects against the most common error after an intense experience, which is believing that something has changed because it felt as though it had.

● Evidence: well-established

Self-judgement is unreliable; blind comparison helps. People often misjudge their own performance (Kruger & Dunning, 1999), and expectation can change performance (Beedie & Foad, 2009). Comparing filmed trials, with an outside judge who does not know which is which, reduces these biases.

Tool 4: Sober replication

The final test of an altered-session insight is whether it can be practised and reproduced sober, over weeks, by the ordinary methods of skill learning. If it can, the altered session pointed to something real. If it cannot, nothing has been lost except a hypothesis.

A useful attitude is to treat the altered session as a scout and the sober practice as the army. The scout can see over the hill. The army has to walk there.

When integration is hard

Not every session leaves behind insights. Some leave behind fear, confusion, or distress. In the survey of challenging psilocybin experiences, 7.6% of those whose experience had happened more than a year earlier had sought treatment for lasting psychological symptoms (Carbonaro et al., 2016). If an experience leaves you anxious, unable to sleep, seeing persistent visual disturbances, or feeling disconnected from yourself or reality, speak to a doctor or mental health professional. There is no shame in it, and it is part of practising responsibly.

⚠ Caution

Give it time. Avoid major life decisions in the days after an intense experience. Do not test an insight in sparring, with weapons, or with heavy implements until it has been reproduced in slow, sober practice. And remember that insights about the world, about other people, or about your own specialness deserve even more scepticism than insights about a spiral.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Integration as practice. The four tools in this chapter are my suggestions. They follow the source document’s integration principles and general research on skill and bias. They have not been tested as a method.

The Same Doors Without the Key: Sober Paths

Chapter 13

Geometric awareness is presented as a lens for refining existing practice, not a replacement for progressive, disciplined training. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

Many of the qualities practitioners hope to find in altered practice can also be approached without any substance at all: a vivid sense of geometry in movement, a quieter inner critic, a deeper feel for the body, a sense of connection. Some of these sober paths have far more research behind them than psilocybin does. For a reader who cannot or will not use psilocybin, and that includes anyone screened out in Chapter 5, this chapter is the way in. For a reader who does practise altered, it is the daily ground that makes the occasional altered session worth anything.

Slow forms and Tai Chi

The research in Chapter 2 is itself a sober path. Tai Chi improves balance and reduces falls (Huang et al., 2017; Sherrington et al., 2019), and long-term practitioners show finer proprioception (Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003; Xu et al., 2004). Movement-based contemplative practices such as yoga, qigong, and Tai Chi are said by their practitioners to cultivate interoceptive, proprioceptive, and kinesthetic awareness at their core (Schmalzl et al., 2014). Every exploration in Chapter 6, the slow form, the circle walk, the spiral tracing, and the eyes-open and eyes-closed comparison, can be done sober, daily, for years.

Meditation and the quiet self

Chapter 3 described how psilocybin reduces activity and connectivity in hubs of the default mode network, the brain system linked to mind-wandering and self-referential thought (Carhart-Harris et al., 2012). Experienced meditators also show reduced activity in main nodes of this network during meditation (Brewer et al., 2011). People’s minds wander a great deal in daily life, and they tend to be less happy when they do (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010).

Meditation’s measured benefits are real but modest. A major systematic review found moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation programmes improve anxiety, depression, and pain, with small-to-moderate effects (Goyal et al., 2014). Claims beyond that, especially about dramatic transformations, are often overstated (Van Dam et al., 2018).

A careful comparison of meditation and psychedelic states concluded that both can disrupt self-consciousness, but that neither is a single uniform category, and that “self-loss” can take several forms, narrative and embodied (Millière et al., 2018). Reviews of self-transcendent experiences, including mindfulness, flow, and awe, characterize them by a decrease in the salience of the self and an increase in feelings of connection (Yaden et al., 2017).

● Evidence: well-established

Meditation has modest, real benefits and quiets the self-referential brain. Mindfulness programmes produce small-to-moderate improvements in anxiety, depression, and pain (Goyal et al., 2014), and experienced meditators show reduced default mode network activity (Brewer et al., 2011). Larger claims are often overstated (Van Dam et al., 2018).

When meditation and psilocybin meet

Two studies have looked at what happens when meditation and psilocybin are combined, both in carefully controlled, supervised research settings.

In a double-blind study of 39 experienced meditators on a five-day mindfulness retreat, psilocybin increased meditation depth and the incidence of positively experienced self-dissolution “without concomitant anxiety,” and produced larger positive changes in psychosocial functioning at four months, compared with placebo. The authors concluded that “meditation seems to enhance psilocybin’s positive effects while counteracting possible dysphoric responses” (Smigielski et al., 2019).

In a randomized trial, healthy volunteers began a programme of meditation and spiritual practice and later received psilocybin or a very low comparison dose. At six months, the higher-dose groups showed large positive changes in measures including interpersonal closeness, gratitude, life meaning, and forgiveness, corroborated by community observers. The determinants of these enduring effects were the mystical-type experience and the rates of meditation and spiritual practice (Griffiths et al., 2018).

These are not studies of martial practice. But they point to the same principle as this book’s integration chapter: what a person practises, before and after, shapes what an altered experience becomes.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Meditation practice may shape and sustain psilocybin’s effects. In supervised research settings, meditation practice was associated with deeper, less anxious experiences and more enduring positive change (Smigielski et al., 2019; Griffiths et al., 2018). These are single studies with selected participants.

Breath

Slow, deliberate breathing is the oldest tool in the internal arts, and one of the best-studied sober practices. A systematic review of slow breathing found that it is associated with changes in heart rate variability, brain activity, and psychological wellbeing, including greater relaxation and less anxiety (Zaccaro et al., 2018). Heart rate variability biofeedback, a structured form of slow breathing, has been proposed to work through the baroreflex, the body’s blood-pressure regulation loop (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). A meta-analysis of twelve randomized trials found that breathwork was associated with lower stress than control conditions, with a small-to-medium effect, and with similar effects on anxiety and depressive symptoms; the authors urge caution about “a miscalibration between hype and evidence” (Fincham et al., 2023).

For a practitioner, breathwork is both a sober path and a safety tool. The same slow breathing that calms the body in daily practice is a way to steady oneself if an altered session becomes frightening.

● Evidence: well-established

Slow breathing and breathwork reduce stress modestly. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses support small-to-medium benefits for stress, anxiety, and mood (Zaccaro et al., 2018; Fincham et al., 2023).

Flow

Flow, the state of effortless absorption in action, may be the sober experience closest to what practitioners describe in altered movement. Research on flow in sport is growing (Swann et al., 2012), and an attentional account proposes that it involves effortless attention, reduced self-referential thinking, and efficient, automatic control of action (Harris et al., 2017). Flow tends to arise when the challenge of an activity is matched to skill, and when attention is fully absorbed. Free form, slow forms, and juggling at the edge of one’s ability are all ordinary ways of inviting it.

Mental imagery

Shadow work and mental practice, described in Chapter 7, are fully available sober. Imagining movement recruits brain networks that overlap with those used in performing it (Hardwick et al., 2018), and mental practice has small but reliable benefits on performance (Driskell et al., 1994; Toth et al., 2020). A practitioner who closes their eyes and slowly imagines a spiral running from the back foot through the hips to the hand is training something real.

A sober practice for every altered one

Every altered exploration in this book has a sober counterpart.
Altered exploration Sober counterpart
Slow form, noticing where turns begin Daily slow form at half speed, with filming
Wide circle walking Daily Baguazhang-style circle walking
Tracing spirals, eyes open and closed Spiral tracing as a daily warm-up
Free form Free movement practice; flow at the edge of skill
Shadow work Slow shadow work; mental imagery
Light juggling Juggling practice with progression
Light touch on bag and dummy Push hands; graded contact training
Inner-sense experiments Body-scan meditation; heartbeat and breath awareness
Quiet of the inner critic Meditation; external focus of attention

None of these sober paths will produce the vivid strangeness of the altered state. But they can be practised every day, safely, legally, alone, and for a lifetime. Most of the measured benefits in this book come from them.

Consciousness, Measured and Unmeasured

Chapter 14

Individual results vary; integration and consistent practice remain essential. — from the source document on geometric expression in the martial arts

I hope these books will help facilitate an upgrade in human consciousness. Of all the fields of science this series has touched, psilocybin research comes closest to studying that hope directly. It has measured experiences that people describe as among the most meaningful of their lives, and lasting changes that follow them. It has also, more than most fields, had to reckon with how hard such things are to measure fairly. This final chapter sets out both.

Experiences of a lifetime

In a landmark double-blind study, 36 hallucinogen-naive adults who regularly took part in religious or spiritual activities received psilocybin and an active comparison drug in supportive conditions. Psilocybin occasioned experiences similar to spontaneously occurring mystical experiences. Two months later, volunteers rated the experience as having substantial personal meaning and spiritual significance and attributed lasting positive changes in attitudes and behaviour to it, changes that were consistent with ratings by community observers (Griffiths et al., 2006). At fourteen months, 58% and 67% of volunteers rated the experience among the five most personally meaningful and most spiritually significant of their lives, respectively, and 64% reported that it had increased their wellbeing or life satisfaction (Griffiths et al., 2008).

Such experiences seem to matter for what follows. Openness to experience, a personality trait usually stable in adulthood, increased after a high-dose psilocybin session, and remained higher more than a year later in participants who had had a mystical experience (MacLean et al., 2011). In patients receiving psilocybin for depression, the strength of the “oceanic boundlessness” dimension of the experience predicted clinical outcomes (Roseman et al., 2018). In a large survey, the link between mystical and insightful experiences and later reductions in depression and anxiety was fully mediated by increases in psychological flexibility (Davis et al., 2020).

● Evidence: well-established

Psilocybin can occasion mystical-type experiences that people rate as among the most meaningful of their lives. Controlled studies with follow-up show sustained personal meaning and attributed positive change, corroborated by observers (Griffiths et al., 2006; Griffiths et al., 2008; MacLean et al., 2011).

In the clinic

Clinical trials have tested psilocybin, given with psychological support, for several conditions. In two randomized trials in people with cancer, psilocybin produced substantial and sustained reductions in depression and anxiety (Griffiths et al., 2016; Ross et al., 2016). In a small trial for major depression with a waiting-list control, effects were large (Davis et al., 2021). In a double-blind comparison with the antidepressant escitalopram, the difference on the primary outcome was not statistically significant (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021). In the largest trial, in 233 people with treatment-resistant depression, the highest dose reduced depression scores more than a very low dose at three weeks, but sustained response at twelve weeks was not clearly supported, and adverse events were common (Goodwin et al., 2022).

The brain that rewires (in mice)

Some of the most-quoted findings about psilocybin and “rewiring” come from animals. In mice, a single dose of psilocybin led to roughly 10% increases in the size and density of dendritic spines, the tiny structures where neurons connect, in the frontal cortex; the growth appeared within 24 hours and persisted a month later (Shao et al., 2021). Psychedelics also promoted the growth of neuron branches and connections in cultured neurons and in animals (Ly et al., 2018).

These are important findings. They are not human findings. Whether anything similar happens in a human practitioner’s brain, and whether it would help or hinder the learning of a movement skill, is unknown.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Neuroplasticity: animal and cell studies only. Psilocybin increased dendritic spine growth in mice (Shao et al., 2021), and psychedelics promoted neural plasticity in cultured neurons and animals (Ly et al., 2018). There is no evidence that this translates into improved skill learning in humans.

The hardest problem: knowing what you know

Psychedelic research has had to confront a problem that also runs through this whole book. When an experience is this vivid, everyone knows who got the real thing.

A review of psychedelic trials argued that their effect sizes are likely overestimated because participants can tell whether they received the drug, and because expectations of benefit are high; most trials had not even measured these confounds (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2021). Another review notes that the effects of a high dose are so pronounced that masking is difficult, and that media hype raises participants’ expectations, making trials “highly susceptible to large placebo and nocebo effects” (Aday et al., 2022).

A striking demonstration comes from microdosing. In a self-blinding study, 191 people who microdosed psychedelics followed instructions to mix real doses with placebos without knowing which was which. Both groups improved on every psychological outcome; the placebo group improved just as much, and the small acute differences could be explained by participants breaking the blind. The authors concluded that the anecdotal benefits of microdosing “can be explained by the placebo effect” (Szigeti et al., 2021).

At the level of the population, a survey of 130,152 adults in the United States found no association between lifetime psychedelic use and mental health problems; in several cases, use was associated with fewer problems (Krebs & Johansen, 2013). Like all such surveys, it cannot establish cause.

● Evidence: well-established

Expectancy and unblinding make psychedelic effects hard to measure. Reviews conclude that trial effect sizes are probably overestimated (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2021; Aday et al., 2022), and in a self-blinding microdosing study, placebo matched the active dose (Szigeti et al., 2021).

What this means for the practitioner

Every limit that applies to psychedelic trials applies more strongly to a single practitioner’s experience on a training floor. You know what you took. You expect it to be meaningful. You want it to teach you something. The experience will amplify your sense of significance. And no one is checking the results blind.

That is not a reason to dismiss the experience. It is the reason for the insight test (Chapter 11), the filmed comparisons (Chapter 12), and the sober practices (Chapter 13). It is also the reason this book keeps its categories so carefully apart:

  • Measured: psilocybin changes perception, self-experience, timing, attention, balance, and touch processing; it can occasion experiences of lasting personal meaning; it carries specific risks.
  • Anecdotal: practitioners, including me, find altered practice “mindbending” and illuminating.
  • Speculative: that psilocybin improves martial skill, sensitivity, or understanding of movement. No controlled study has tested this, and there is no direct evidence for it.

An upgrade, honestly described

What, then, might an upgrade in consciousness mean in a book like this?

It might mean what the mystical-experience research describes: moments of unusual meaning, connection, and openness that people carry with them for years. It might mean what my philosophy describes: understanding one’s own mind and body more truly, by studying them directly in an unusual state. And it might mean something the evidence supports better than either: a practitioner who can hold an extraordinary experience lightly, test it honestly, and keep only what proves true.

The source document ends its safety section with a sentence that could stand for the whole series: “Individual results vary; integration and consistent practice remain essential.” Curiosity opens the door. Care keeps it safe. And practice, sober and patient and repeated, is how anything found on the other side becomes yours.

Curiosity opens the door. Care keeps it safe. Practice makes it yours.

  • Light touch (Chapter 8): leaning on the bag, following its swing, slow tracing around the dummy’s arms, self-touch.
  • Inner-sense experiments (Chapter 9): mirror arms, weight centre, heartbeat counting, breath edges, the spiral inside, one-minute estimate, the self in the body.

Appendix B · The Evidence at a Glance

A summary of the main claims discussed in this book, how strong the evidence is, and where to look. “●” marks well-established findings, “◐” suggestive or emerging ones, and “○” claims that are untested or anecdotal.

Claim Strength Key sources
Tai Chi improves balance and reduces falls in older adults ● Established Huang et al., 2017; Sherrington et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018
Long-term Tai Chi practitioners have better proprioception ● Established (cross-sectional) Tsang & Hui-Chan, 2003; Xu et al., 2004
Baguazhang, Wing Chun, and push hands have been studied ◐ A few small studies Cao & Zhang, 2026; Fuchs et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2010
Wooden dummy training has measurable effects ○ No studies Chapter 8
Martial arts loading can strengthen forearm bone ◐ One non-randomized study Khalil et al., 2023
Psilocybin alters perception and self via 5-HT2A ● Established Vollenweider et al., 1998; Kometer et al., 2013
Psilocybin geometry reflects visual cortex architecture ◐ Strong model, plus EEG evidence Bressloff et al., 2001; Kometer et al., 2013
Entropic brain, REBUS, ALBUS ◐ Hypotheses Carhart-Harris et al., 2014; Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019; Safron et al., 2025
Psilocybin impairs timing, attention, psychomotor performance, balance ● Established Wittmann et al., 2007; Hasler et al., 2004; Barrett et al., 2018; Carbonaro et al., 2018
Psilocybin alters processing of touch and bodily self ◐ One imaging study, theory Duerler et al., 2021; Ho et al., 2020
Psilocybin improves martial or athletic skill ○ No evidence Portes et al., 2025
Practising altered teaches the mind and body ○ Practitioner philosophy Foreword; Chapter 1
Support and setting reduce harm ● Established Johnson et al., 2008; Carbonaro et al., 2016; Kopra et al., 2022
Psychosis or bipolar family history increases risk ◐ Survey and guideline evidence Johnson et al., 2008; Simonsson et al., 2025
Lithium with psychedelics risks seizures ◐ Case reports, consistent Nayak et al., 2021
HPPD is uncommon but real ◐ Limited data Halpern & Pope, 2003; Doyle et al., 2022
Experts perceive in chunks and templates ● Established Chase & Simon, 1973; Gobet & Simon, 1996
Brains learn statistical patterns automatically ● Established Saffran et al., 1996; Fiser & Aslin, 2001
Combat experts anticipate from early cues ● Established Mann et al., 2007; Mori et al., 2002; Milazzo et al., 2016
Expectation and need for control produce false patterns ● Established Liu et al., 2014; Whitson & Galinsky, 2008
Psychedelics amplify meaning ◐ LSD study and theory Preller et al., 2017; Hartogsohn, 2018
Psilocybin can occasion lasting meaningful experiences ● Established (small, selected samples) Griffiths et al., 2006; Griffiths et al., 2008
Psilocybin builds new neural connections ◐ Animals and cells only Shao et al., 2021; Ly et al., 2018
Psychedelic trial effects are overestimated by expectancy ◐ Strong methodological case Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2021; Aday et al., 2022; Szigeti et al., 2021
Meditation and breathwork have modest benefits ● Established Goyal et al., 2014; Fincham et al., 2023
Meditation shapes psilocybin outcomes ◐ Two studies Smigielski et al., 2019; Griffiths et al., 2018

Glossary

5-HT2A receptor — A serotonin receptor in the brain. Psilocybin’s main psychedelic effects depend on stimulating it.

ALBUS — “Altered beliefs under psychedelics,” a hypothesis that psychedelics can either relax or strengthen the brain’s prior expectations, depending on conditions.

Angular momentum — The rotational equivalent of momentum, which stays constant unless an outside twisting force acts.

Apophenia — Perceiving meaningful connections between unrelated things.

Chunk — A meaningful group of information or movements that is perceived, remembered, or executed as a unit.

Default mode network — A set of brain regions, including parts of the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex, associated with self-related thought and mind-wandering.

Ego dissolution — A temporary loss or weakening of the ordinary sense of self, measured in psychedelic research by questionnaires.

Entropic brain hypothesis — The proposal that psychedelic states involve increased variability (“entropy”) of brain activity, and that ordinary waking consciousness suppresses it.

Expectancy — The influence of what a person expects on what they experience and report.

Flow — A state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, in which self-consciousness fades and action feels effortless.

Form constants — Klüver’s four categories of geometric hallucination: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels and funnels, and spirals.

HPPD — Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder: recurring perceptual disturbances long after a hallucinogen has worn off.

Integration — The work done after an experience to make sense of it and carry what is valuable into ordinary life and practice.

Interoception — The sense of what is happening inside the body, such as heartbeat, breath, and gut sensations. Accuracy, sensibility, and awareness are distinct dimensions.

Mook yan jong — The Wing Chun wooden dummy.

Mystical-type experience — An experience characterized by unity, sacredness, deeply felt positive mood, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability, measured by questionnaires.

Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful shapes, such as faces, in random or ambiguous stimuli.

Perceptual learning — Improvement in sensory abilities through practice.

Proprioception — The sense of the position and movement of the body’s parts.

Psilocybin — A compound produced by several species of mushroom, converted in the body to psilocin, which acts mainly on 5-HT2A receptors.

Push hands — A two-person Tai Chi practice of maintaining contact while yielding to and redirecting a partner’s force.

REBUS — “Relaxed beliefs under psychedelics,” a model proposing that psychedelics relax the precision of high-level expectations, freeing bottom-up information.

Rotational inertia — Resistance to changes in rotation, increased by mass far from the axis.

Set and setting — The mindset a person brings to an experience, and the physical and social environment in which it happens.

Sitter — A sober, trusted person who stays with someone in an altered state to keep them and the space safe.

Statistical learning — Automatic learning of the regularities in a stream of experience, such as which sounds or shapes tend to occur together.

Template — In expertise research, a large long-term memory structure into which new information can be slotted rapidly.

About This Book

Title. Lens and Lattice: Altered Perception, the Internal Arts, and the Science of a Curious Practice. Book 4 of the Companions to the System of Inevitability.

Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. First edition, November 2026.

Also in this series. Book 1: Walking and Turning: Iron, Spirals, and the Science of a Practicing Mind, on the iron balls, the ring bar, and the brain science of juggling and skill. Book 2: Wave and Return: The Bent Fist, the Figure-Eight, and the Science of a Restrained Hand, on the system’s striking, breath, safe progression, testing, and the ethics of restraint. Book 3: Shape and Choice: Everyday Geometry, Calm Presence, and the Science of a Choosing Mind, on the system’s philosophy of everyday geometry, presence, and keeping choice inside automatic skill. Book 5: Nucleus and Orbit: Atoms, Necessity, and the Science of an Interwoven Practice, on the system’s atomism, its 3-6-9 architecture, and its quantum language set beside the real science of atoms, necessity, chaos, the fractal body, and interdependence, tying the series together. The series continues.

About this book. Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. The testimony and philosophy of altered practice in this book are my own. This book does not recommend that anyone use any substance. The source document on geometric expression in the martial arts, compiled in November 2026, names no specific system. All practices, safeguards, tests, and logs are my suggestions, drawn from the general scientific literature.

Method. Every peer-reviewed study cited was checked against its Crossref record (authors, year, title, journal, volume, pages, DOI), and the specific findings reported were checked against the published abstracts. Where no abstract was available, the study is cited only for what its title and record establish, and no numbers are given. Numbers are reported as the original authors reported them. Drug doses used in studies are deliberately omitted. Animal and cell studies are identified as such. Where a claim is untested, the text says so. No quotations have been invented; quotations from the source materials are reproduced as written.

Illustrations. The plates are original geometric studies created for this book. The form-constant schematics are simplified drawings of categories described in the scientific literature, not reproductions of any figure. No figure depicts any real person.

Typography. Set in EB Garamond and Cormorant Garamond, with Inter for labels.

Not advice. Nothing in this book is medical, psychological, or legal advice, and nothing in it encourages the use of any drug. Psilocybin is illegal in most places. This book contains no information on doses, sources, or preparation.

Corrections. Science moves. If you find an error, or a new study that bears on anything here, please share it, and share a corrected copy under the same license.
